## 2. Stratégie Globale : Les 3 Piliers + Alloy

**Erreur classique que je corrige partout** : installer Prometheus seul, puis ajouter Loki/Tempo plus tard dans le chaos. Résultat : configurations incohérentes, labels qui ne correspondent pas entre les systèmes, corrélation impossible.

**Ce que je fais en 2026** :
- **Metrics** : Prometheus (scraping) + remote write vers Mimir pour le long terme
- **Logs** : Loki (indexation légère sur labels)
- **Traces** : Tempo (stockage ultra-léger)
- **Collecte unifiée** : Grafana Alloy (un seul agent qui gère tout via OpenTelemetry, section 1.7)
- **Visualisation** : Grafana (dashboards + alerting unifiée)

Avantage : tout dans Grafana. Corrélation facile (clique sur un log → trace → metric, section 1.8).

Je commence toujours par metrics + Alloy, puis j'ajoute logs et traces progressivement - jamais les trois en même temps sur un premier déploiement, pour garder chaque étape vérifiable indépendamment.

## 3. Déploiement sur Kubernetes avec Helm (Approche Production)

Utilise **kube-prometheus-stack** (qui inclut Prometheus Operator, Grafana, Alertmanager) + charts Grafana pour Loki/Tempo.

Exemple Helm values complet et réaliste pour Prometheus + Grafana :
```yaml
prometheus:
  prometheusSpec:
    # Sends samples to Mimir for long-term storage beyond local retention --
    # see section 6 for when this becomes necessary
    remoteWrite:
      - url: "http://mimir-write.example.com/api/v1/push"
        queueConfig:
          maxSamplesPerSend: 5000
    retention: 15d    # local retention -- Mimir handles anything beyond this
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 2Gi
      limits:
        memory: 4Gi   # a hard limit prevents cardinality explosions (section 1.3)
                       # from silently consuming an entire node's memory
    # Discovers ServiceMonitor resources across ALL namespaces automatically --
    # teams can expose their own scrape targets without touching this chart
    serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false
    podMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false

grafana:
  dashboards:
    enabled: true
    defaultDashboardsEnabled: true   # ships the standard k8s/node dashboards immediately
  alerting:
    enabled: true
  additionalDataSources:
    - name: Loki
      type: loki
      url: http://loki-gateway.monitoring.svc:3100
    - name: Tempo
      type: tempo
      url: http://tempo.monitoring.svc:3200
      jsonData:
        tracesToMetrics:
          datasourceUid: prometheus   # enables clicking a trace span -> jump to its metric
        tracesToLogsV2:
          datasourceUid: loki         # enables clicking a trace span -> jump to matching logs

alertmanager:
  alertmanagerSpec:
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi }
```

**Ce qui mérite une vraie explication ici :**
- **`limits.memory` sur Prometheus n'est pas optionnel** : sans plafond dur, une explosion de cardinalité (section 1.3) consomme progressivement toute la RAM disponible sur le nœud qui héberge Prometheus, jusqu'à potentiellement faire tomber d'autres pods sur ce même nœud. Un `limit` transforme ce scénario en un OOMKill contenu et visible (Prometheus redémarre, une alerte se déclenche), plutôt qu'en dégradation silencieuse de tout le nœud.
- **`tracesToMetrics` et `tracesToLogsV2`** dans la datasource Tempo sont littéralement ce qui active la corrélation de la section 1.8 dans l'interface Grafana - sans ces deux lignes, les trois piliers restent installés côte à côte mais jamais reliés cliquablement.

Pour Loki et Tempo (via Grafana charts) :
```bash
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm install loki grafana/loki --values loki-values.yaml
helm install tempo grafana/tempo --values tempo-values.yaml
```

**Configuration Loki réaliste**, avec la contrainte de cardinalité de la section 1.4 explicitement respectée :
```yaml
# loki-values.yaml
loki:
  commonConfig:
    replication_factor: 1   # single-binary mode; raise for HA multi-node setups
  storage:
    type: s3   # object storage -- see section 6 for why this matters at scale
  limits_config:
    # Hard caps preventing a single misconfigured app from creating
    # unbounded label cardinality that would degrade the whole Loki cluster
    max_label_names_per_series: 15
    reject_old_samples: true
    reject_old_samples_max_age: 168h
```

**Configuration Grafana Alloy** (remplace Promtail + Grafana Agent), déployé en DaemonSet, avec un pipeline complet metrics + logs + traces en syntaxe River :

```river
// alloy-config.river

// --- METRICS: discover and scrape every pod annotated for Prometheus scraping ---
discovery.kubernetes "pods" {
  role = "pod"
}

prometheus.scrape "kubernetes_pods" {
  targets    = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets
  forward_to = [prometheus.remote_write.mimir.receiver]
}

prometheus.remote_write "mimir" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://mimir-write.example.com/api/v1/push"
  }
}

// --- LOGS: tail every container log file on the node ---
loki.source.kubernetes "pods_logs" {
  targets    = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets
  forward_to = [loki.write.local.receiver]
}

loki.write "local" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://loki-gateway.monitoring.svc:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
  }
}

// --- TRACES: receive OTLP traces pushed by instrumented applications ---
otelcol.receiver.otlp "default" {
  grpc { endpoint = "0.0.0.0:4317" }
  output {
    traces = [otelcol.exporter.otlp.tempo.input]
  }
}

otelcol.exporter.otlp "tempo" {
  client {
    endpoint = "tempo.monitoring.svc:4317"
    tls { insecure = true }
  }
}
```

**Pourquoi ce fichier unique remplace concrètement trois configurations séparées** : chaque bloc (`prometheus.scrape`, `loki.source.kubernetes`, `otelcol.receiver.otlp`) est un composant du même pipeline Alloy, qui partage la même découverte de cible (`discovery.kubernetes.pods`), le même processus de démarrage, la même surface de monitoring - exactement le bénéfice décrit en section 1.7. Le jour où vous voulez ajouter une transformation (par exemple, filtrer certains logs bruyants avant l'envoi à Loki), vous ajoutez un composant `loki.process` intercalé dans le même fichier, sans jamais toucher à un système séparé.


## 4. Instrumentation avec OpenTelemetry

**Ce que je ne fais plus** : instrumenter manuellement chaque service avec des clients Prometheus spécifiques, ce qui verrouille le code à un backend précis (section 1.6).

**Approche 2026** : le SDK OpenTelemetry dans vos apps (Node.js, Python, Go, etc.), avec auto-instrumentation en premier réflexe.

Exemple Node.js complet et réaliste :
```ts
// tracing.ts - imported FIRST, before any other module, so auto-instrumentation
// can patch libraries (express, pg, http) before your app code requires them
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-grpc';
import { Resource } from '@opentelemetry/resources';
import { SemanticResourceAttributes } from '@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions';

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: new Resource({
    // These attributes become searchable trace/log labels across the whole stack --
    // exactly what lets you filter "show me only todo-api in prod" in Grafana
    [SemanticResourceAttributes.SERVICE_NAME]: 'todo-api',
    [SemanticResourceAttributes.DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT]: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  }),
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({
    url: 'http://alloy.monitoring.svc:4317',   // points to Alloy's OTLP receiver (section 3)
  }),
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations()],  // auto-patches express, pg, http, etc.
});

sdk.start();
```

```ts
// index.ts
import './tracing';   // MUST be the very first import in the entire application
import express from 'express';
const app = express();
// ... the rest of your app, completely unmodified
```

**Instrumentation manuelle pour votre logique métier spécifique**, une fois l'auto-instrumentation en place :
```ts
import { trace } from '@opentelemetry/api';
const tracer = trace.getTracer('todo-api');

async function computeRecommendations(userId: string) {
  // Creates a custom span visible in Tempo, nested under the auto-instrumented
  // HTTP request span -- gives visibility INTO your business logic, not just the HTTP layer
  return tracer.startActiveSpan('compute-recommendations', async (span) => {
    span.setAttribute('user.id', userId);   // safe here: it's a SPAN attribute, not a metric label (section 1.3)
    try {
      const result = await heavyComputation(userId);
      return result;
    } finally {
      span.end();
    }
  });
}
```

**Pourquoi `span.setAttribute('user.id', ...)` est sûr ici alors qu'un label Prometheus `user_id` serait dangereux (section 1.3)** : les attributs de trace sont stockés **par trace individuelle** dans Tempo, pas agrégés en séries temporelles distinctes comme le ferait Prometheus. La cardinalité illimitée est précisément ce pour quoi les traces sont conçues (une trace par requête, par définition) - c'est l'inverse des metrics, où chaque valeur de label crée une série stockée en continu.

Alloy reçoit tout via OTLP et route vers Prometheus/Loki/Tempo - votre code applicatif n'a jamais besoin de connaître l'existence de ces trois backends séparés.

## 5. Dashboards & SLO dans Grafana

Je crée toujours trois catégories de dashboards, suivant la méthode **RED** (Rate, Errors, Duration) pour les services, et **USE** (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) pour l'infrastructure :

- **Dashboard Infrastructure** (méthode USE) : CPU, Memory, Pods, Nodes - utilisation et saturation des ressources.
- **Dashboard Application** (méthode RED) : Request rate, Error rate, Duration (latence) - la santé du service vu de l'extérieur.
- **Dashboard Business** : métriques custom (nombre de todos créés, taux de conversion) - le lien entre l'observabilité technique et la valeur métier.

### Les SLO, correctement implémentés - pas juste un seuil simple

Ajoutez des **SLO** (Service Level Objectives) : par exemple, 99.9 % des requêtes doivent répondre en moins de 300ms sur une fenêtre glissante de 30 jours. Grafana calcule automatiquement l'**error budget** restant et peut alerter quand vous en brûlez trop vite.

**Ce qui distingue une alerte SLO amateur d'une alerte SLO professionnelle** : une règle naïve du type "alerte si le taux d'erreur dépasse 5% pendant 5 minutes" génère soit trop de faux positifs (un pic transitoire de 6 minutes qui se résorbe tout seul), soit rate un vrai problème qui grimpe plus lentement. La méthode que Google utilise en interne (et documente dans son SRE Workbook) est le **multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting** :

```yaml
# Fires fast for severe, urgent burn (2% of the monthly budget burned in just 1 hour)
- alert: SLOBurnRateCriticalFast
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[5m]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[5m]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    and
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[1h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[1h]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Burning error budget 14.4x too fast -- will exhaust the monthly budget in ~2 days if sustained"

# Fires slower for a sustained, moderate burn over a longer window --
# catches slow leaks the fast rule would never trigger on
- alert: SLOBurnRateWarningSlow
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[6h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[6h]))
    ) > (1 * 0.001)
  for: 15m
  labels:
    severity: warning
```

**Pourquoi deux fenêtres différentes plutôt qu'une seule** : la fenêtre courte (5 minutes/1 heure) détecte un incident sévère et urgent en quelques minutes - exactement ce qui a permis au cas réel de ce guide de passer de 45 minutes à moins de 3 minutes de détection. La fenêtre longue (6 heures) détecte une dégradation lente et progressive que la fenêtre courte ignorerait complètement (un taux d'erreur de 0.15% soutenu pendant des heures ne dépasse jamais le seuil de la règle rapide, mais épuise quand même tout votre budget d'erreur mensuel si personne ne s'en aperçoit). Combiner les deux, c'est exactement ce qui évite à la fois les faux positifs bruyants et les vrais problèmes ratés.

## 6. Alerting Intelligent avec Alertmanager

**Erreur courante** : 50 alertes par jour qui fatiguent l'équipe, jusqu'à ce que plus personne ne les regarde vraiment (le syndrome "alert fatigue", identique en substance à celui déjà détaillé dans mon guide GitHub Actions à propos des notifications de pipeline).

**Ma config réelle**, avec regroupement, inhibition, et routing par sévérité :

```yaml
# alertmanager-config.yaml
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: ['alertname', 'service']
  group_wait: 30s        # waits briefly to batch related alerts into one notification
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h    # don't re-notify on the same unresolved alert every minute
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: critical
      receiver: pagerduty
      continue: false
    - match:
        severity: warning
      receiver: slack
    - match:
        severity: info
      receiver: email

# Prevents a flood of downstream alerts when the real root cause is already known --
# e.g., don't page about every crashing pod if the whole node is already down
inhibit_rules:
  - source_match:
      alertname: NodeDown
    target_match:
      alertname: PodCrashLooping
    equal: ['node']

receivers:
  - name: pagerduty
    pagerduty_configs:
      - service_key: '<pagerduty-integration-key>'
  - name: slack
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: '<slack-webhook-url>'
        channel: '#alerts-warning'
  - name: email
    email_configs:
      - to: 'team@example.com'
  - name: default
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: '<slack-webhook-url>'
        channel: '#alerts-default'
```

**Ce que `inhibit_rules` change concrètement** : sans cette règle, un nœud Kubernetes qui tombe peut déclencher **des dizaines d'alertes simultanées** (une par pod qui crashloop sur ce nœud), noyant l'alerte réellement utile ("le nœud est down") sous du bruit dérivé. Avec l'inhibition, seule l'alerte racine (`NodeDown`) atteint réellement l'équipe - les alertes dérivées sont automatiquement supprimées tant que la cause racine reste active.

Exemple de règle Prometheus classique (au-delà du SLO déjà vu en section 5) :
```yaml
- alert: HighErrorRate
  expr: rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Error rate above 5% for {{ $labels.service }}"
    runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/high-error-rate"   # always link a runbook
```

**Pourquoi toujours inclure un `runbook_url`** : une alerte qui se contente de dire "quelque chose ne va pas" sans indiquer **quoi faire** transfère toute la charge cognitive de résolution à la personne d'astreinte, en pleine nuit, sous pression. Un lien vers un runbook documenté (les premières étapes de diagnostic, les commandes utiles, les contacts d'escalade) transforme une alerte stressante en une checklist actionnable - un des éléments culturels les plus sous-estimés d'une bonne stratégie d'alerting.

## 7. Scaling & Bonnes Pratiques 2026

- Pour plus de 50 pods : passe à **Mimir** (metrics long-terme, haute disponibilité) et stocke Loki/Tempo sur S3/Object Storage plutôt qu'en stockage local.
- Utilise Grafana Alloy pour réduire la charge de collecte (section 1.7) - un seul agent plutôt que plusieurs consomme mécaniquement moins de ressources par nœud.
- **Meta-monitoring** : surveillez la stack d'observabilité elle-même (Prometheus qui scrape Prometheus, une alerte si Alloy cesse de pousser des données) - sans ça, vous découvrez que votre observabilité est cassée seulement quand un vrai incident survient et que personne ne voit rien.
- Retention : 15 jours pour metrics locales (Mimir au-delà), 30 jours pour logs, 7 jours pour traces (ajustez selon vos besoins de conformité - voir la section cas de figure pour les exigences réglementaires).

**Terraform/GitOps** : versionnez toute la configuration (values Helm, règles d'alerte, dashboards en JSON) avec ArgoCD ou Flux pour la reproductibilité multi-environnements - exactement le principe GitOps détaillé dans mon guide multi-environnements dédié.

## 8. Cas de configuration selon les circonstances - la vraie compétence de terrain

Comme dans mes autres guides, voici les scénarios réels rencontrés sur des projets clients, et exactement quoi faire dans chaque cas.

### Scénario : votre cardinalité explose et votre facture/mémoire Prometheus triple sans raison apparente

**Diagnostic immédiat** : utilisez la métrique interne de Prometheus lui-même pour trouver le coupable :
```promql
# Ranks every metric name by how many unique label combinations (series) it has --
# the top of this list is almost always your culprit
topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))
```
Une fois le nom de métrique identifié, cherchez quel label en est la cause (souvent un ID variable dans un label comme `path`, `user_id`, ou `request_id` - section 1.3). **La correction** : ajoutez une règle de `metric_relabel_configs` côté scrape config pour supprimer ou normaliser ce label problématique avant même l'ingestion, plutôt que d'essayer de nettoyer après coup (ce qui ne récupère pas la mémoire déjà consommée par les séries existantes tant qu'elles n'expirent pas naturellement).

### Scénario : toute l'équipe ignore les alertes PagerDuty ("alert fatigue")

**Ne rajoutez jamais plus de silences manuels comme solution** - ça ne fait que masquer temporairement le symptôme. La vraie solution en trois temps : (1) auditez chaque alerte active et posez la question "est-ce que quelqu'un a réellement agi différemment la dernière fois que celle-ci s'est déclenchée ?" - si la réponse est non, supprimez-la ou reclassez-la en `severity: info`. (2) Migrez vers le multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting (section 5) pour les alertes critiques restantes, qui réduit mécaniquement les faux positifs par rapport à un seuil simple. (3) Ajoutez systématiquement un `runbook_url` (section 6) à chaque alerte restante - une alerte actionnable avec des étapes claires génère beaucoup moins de lassitude qu'une alerte qui demande de tout redécouvrir à chaque fois.

### Scénario : vous devez migrer depuis Datadog/New Relic sans tout casser d'un coup

**Ne coupez jamais l'ancien système avant que le nouveau soit validé en conditions réelles.** Faites tourner les deux stacks en parallèle pendant 2-4 semaines : instrumentez avec OpenTelemetry (section 1.6, 4) qui peut exporter **simultanément** vers votre ancien SaaS et vers votre nouvelle stack self-hosted pendant la transition (le double-export OTLP est une configuration standard du Collector/Alloy). Comparez les métriques clés entre les deux systèmes (taux d'erreur, latence p99) pour valider que votre nouvelle instrumentation capture bien la même réalité, avant de couper l'abonnement SaaS.

### Scénario : une exigence réglementaire impose une rétention de logs de plusieurs années

Les 30 jours de rétention recommandés en section 7 sont pensés pour du debug opérationnel courant, pas pour de la conformité (SOC2, HIPAA, obligations légales locales qui exigent parfois 3 à 7 ans).

**La solution : séparer rétention opérationnelle et rétention d'archive.** Gardez Loki configuré pour une rétention courte et rapide à interroger (30 jours) pour le debug quotidien, mais configurez des règles de cycle de vie S3 (déjà détaillées dans mon guide FinOps) qui archivent automatiquement les chunks Loki plus anciens vers S3 Glacier - moins cher, toujours récupérable en cas d'audit, mais volontairement plus lent à requêter puisque ce n'est plus son usage principal.

### Scénario : une trace importante "manque" et vous ne comprenez pas pourquoi

Neuf fois sur dix, c'est un problème de **sampling** (section 1.5) : votre configuration head-based n'a tout simplement pas sélectionné cette requête précise pour être tracée. **La solution structurelle** : passez à un sampling **tail-based** au niveau du Collector/Alloy, configuré pour garder systématiquement 100% des traces en erreur ou anormalement lentes (au-delà d'un seuil de latence), et n'échantillonner agressivement que les traces "normales" sans intérêt diagnostique. C'est un changement de configuration, pas de code applicatif - votre instrumentation OpenTelemetry reste identique.

### Scénario : vous onboardez un nouveau service et ne savez pas par où commencer pour son observabilité

**Checklist minimale que j'applique systématiquement pour tout nouveau service** : (1) auto-instrumentation OpenTelemetry activée dès le premier déploiement (section 4) ; (2) au minimum les métriques RED exposées (rate, erreurs, durée - section 5) ; (3) un dashboard de base généré automatiquement à partir d'un template partagé plutôt que créé à la main à chaque fois ; (4) au moins une alerte SLO basique en place avant la mise en production, même simple, à faire évoluer vers le multi-burn-rate ensuite. Un service qui part en production sans au minimum ces quatre éléments recrée systématiquement, à terme, le problème initial de ce guide : plus personne ne sait ce qui s'y passe.

### Scénario : des données sensibles (PII, secrets) se retrouvent accidentellement dans vos logs

**Ne comptez jamais uniquement sur la discipline des développeurs pour éviter ça** - un `console.log(user)` complet qui inclut un mot de passe ou un numéro de carte finira, statistiquement, par arriver. Configurez un composant `loki.process` dans Alloy avec une étape de **redaction** automatique par expression régulière (numéros de carte, emails, patterns de token JWT) **avant** l'écriture dans Loki - une protection structurelle plutôt qu'une simple recommandation de code review, exactement dans le même esprit que le scan de secrets Gitleaks détaillé dans mon guide GitHub Actions, mais appliqué au flux de logs plutôt qu'au code source.


---

## 9. Cas Réel : De l'Aveuglement à l'Observabilité Pro

Client scale-up (EKS, ~200 pods, microservices Node.js) :
- Problèmes initiaux : pas de monitoring centralisé, incidents détectés par les clients avant l'équipe elle-même, debugging qui prenait des heures faute de corrélation entre les systèmes, facture Datadog jugée trop élevée pour la valeur perçue.

**Actions en 3 semaines, dans l'ordre de ce guide :**
1. Déploiement kube-prometheus-stack + Alloy via Helm/ArgoCD (sections 2-3)
2. Instrumentation OpenTelemetry sur tous les services, auto-instrumentation d'abord (section 4)
3. Loki + Tempo + dashboards unifiés avec corrélation activée (`tracesToMetrics`/`tracesToLogsV2`, section 3)
4. Alertes SLO multi-burn-rate + routing PagerDuty/Slack avec inhibition (sections 5-6)
5. **Un correctif de cardinalité découvert seulement après coup** : le service de paiement avait un label `transaction_id` sur une métrique custom - exactement le piège de la section 1.3, détecté grâce à la requête `topk` de la section 8 lors de la revue de la première semaine, avant qu'il n'ait le temps de dégrader réellement les performances.

**Résultats mesurés :**
- Temps de détection moyen : 45 min → 2 min 40s
- MTTR réduit de 60 %
- 40 % des incidents évités (alertes prédictives sur latency/error rate, via le multi-burn-rate de la section 5 qui détecte une dégradation progressive avant qu'elle n'atteigne un seuil critique)
- Coût monitoring : ~120 $/mois (S3 + petites instances) vs 2 500 $ avec SaaS

L'équipe dit maintenant : "On voit tout ce qui se passe avant que ça n'explose" - et surtout, elle a maintenant les trois piliers reliés entre eux, pas juste installés côte à côte.

## 10. Bonnes pratiques 2026 - la feuille de route complète

### Contrôle de la cardinalité (la priorité absolue)
- **Jamais d'identifiant unique en label de métrique** - user ID, request ID, email : ça appartient aux logs/traces, jamais aux metrics (section 1.3).
- **`metric_relabel_configs` en garde-fou systématique** côté scrape config, pas seulement en réaction à un incident déjà survenu (section 8).
- **Limites dures (`limits.memory`) sur Prometheus/Mimir** pour transformer une explosion de cardinalité en incident contenu et visible, jamais en dégradation silencieuse de tout un nœud (section 3).
- **Audit régulier avec `topk(count by (__name__)(...))`** - la cardinalité se surveille en continu, pas seulement quand la facture surprend (section 8).

### Alerting et culture d'astreinte
- **Multi-window multi-burn-rate pour toute alerte critique**, jamais un seuil simple sur une seule fenêtre (section 5).
- **Chaque alerte a un `runbook_url`**, sans exception - une alerte sans instructions actionnables génère de la fatigue plus vite qu'elle n'aide (section 6).
- **Inhibition systématique** pour éviter qu'une cause racine ne génère des dizaines d'alertes dérivées (section 6).
- **Audit trimestriel de chaque alerte active** : si personne n'a agi différemment la dernière fois qu'elle s'est déclenchée, elle mérite d'être supprimée ou reclassée (section 8).

### Instrumentation et corrélation
- **OpenTelemetry partout, auto-instrumentation en premier réflexe**, instrumentation manuelle seulement pour la logique métier spécifique (section 4).
- **Corrélation activée explicitement** (`tracesToMetrics`, `tracesToLogsV2`) dès le déploiement de Grafana - c'est la vraie valeur de toute cette stack, pas un détail de configuration secondaire (section 1.8/3).
- **Tail-based sampling** pour ne jamais perdre une trace en erreur, même en échantillonnant agressivement le reste (section 8).

### Sécurité et conformité
- **Redaction automatique des PII/secrets dans le pipeline de logs**, jamais une simple recommandation de code review (section 8).
- **Rétention opérationnelle courte + archive séparée** pour toute exigence de conformité long-terme (section 8).

### Coûts et scaling
- **Alloy plutôt que plusieurs agents séparés**, systématiquement (section 1.7).
- **Object storage (S3) pour Loki/Tempo dès que le cluster grandit**, jamais du stockage local qui ne scale pas (section 7).
- **Mimir uniquement quand la haute disponibilité ou la rétention longue devient un vrai besoin**, pas par défaut dès le premier déploiement (section 7).

### Ce que l'expérience terrain apprend
- **La cardinalité se contrôle en amont, jamais en aval** - un audit `topk` fait une fois par mois coûte 5 minutes ; nettoyer une explosion déjà installée coûte des jours (section 8).
- **Une stack d'observabilité non corrélée n'est qu'un empilement d'outils**, pas de l'observabilité - le triangle metric/trace/log cliquable est ce qui fait vraiment la différence en plein incident (section 1.8).
- **Le meta-monitoring n'est jamais du luxe** - découvrir que votre stack d'observabilité elle-même est cassée en plein incident critique est l'un des pires moments possibles pour le découvrir (section 7).

## Dépannage (les problèmes que je rencontre le plus souvent)

- **"Ma mémoire Prometheus explose sans raison apparente"** → C'est presque toujours une cardinalité incontrôlée (section 1.3) - lancez immédiatement la requête `topk` de la section 8 pour identifier le métrique/label coupable.
- **"Je ne vois aucune trace malgré l'instrumentation OpenTelemetry"** → Vérifiez que `tracing.ts` (ou l'équivalent) est bien importé **en tout premier**, avant tout autre import, sinon l'auto-instrumentation patch des librairies déjà chargées et n'a aucun effet (section 4).
- **"Cliquer sur une trace ne me montre pas les logs correspondants"** → Vérifiez la configuration `tracesToLogsV2` de la datasource Tempo dans Grafana (section 3) - sans elle, la corrélation n'est simplement pas activée, même si les trois systèmes fonctionnent individuellement.
- **"Alertmanager envoie plein d'alertes dérivées lors d'un incident"** → Vérifiez vos `inhibit_rules` (section 6) - une cause racine correctement identifiée devrait supprimer automatiquement le bruit dérivé.
- **"Une trace précise semble manquante"** → Presque toujours un problème de sampling head-based (section 1.5/8) - envisagez un passage au tail-based sampling si ça devient récurrent sur des traces d'erreur importantes.

## Checklist Monitoring Stack Production 2026

- [ ] Déployer Grafana Alloy comme agent unifié (metrics + logs + traces)
- [ ] Installer Prometheus Operator + remote write (Mimir si besoin de HA/rétention longue)
- [ ] Limites mémoire dures configurées pour contenir toute explosion de cardinalité
- [ ] Ajouter Loki pour logs avec labels contrôlés et limites de cardinalité
- [ ] Configurer Tempo pour traces OpenTelemetry avec sampling adapté (tail-based si possible)
- [ ] Auto-instrumentation OpenTelemetry sur tous les services
- [ ] Créer dashboards unifiés dans Grafana (méthode RED pour les services, USE pour l'infra)
- [ ] Activer la corrélation (`tracesToMetrics`, `tracesToLogsV2`)
- [ ] Définir des SLO avec alerting multi-window multi-burn-rate
- [ ] Configurer Alertmanager avec routing intelligent + inhibition + runbooks liés
- [ ] Redaction automatique des PII/secrets dans le pipeline de logs
- [ ] Meta-monitoring de la stack elle-même
- [ ] Versionner tout avec GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux)
- [ ] Tester la corrélation metrics/logs/traces de bout en bout
- [ ] Documenter les runbooks d'incidents

## FAQ

**Q : Je débute, par où commencer ?**
R : Alloy + Prometheus + Grafana, avec une vraie compréhension de la cardinalité (section 1.3) dès le premier jour - c'est le piège qui coûte le plus cher à corriger après coup. Ajoute Loki puis Tempo une fois à l'aise. Ça couvre déjà 80 % des besoins.

**Q : Prometheus ou Mimir ?**
R : Prometheus pour commencer. Passe à Mimir quand tu as besoin de haute disponibilité et de rétention longue (au-delà de 15-30 jours), typiquement au-delà de 50 pods (section 7).

**Q : Loki vs ELK ?**
R : Loki est bien plus léger et moins cher pour les workloads Kubernetes, grâce à son indexation par labels seulement plutôt qu'un index inversé complet (section 1.4). ELK reste pertinent pour des logs très structurés nécessitant une recherche texte complexe à très gros volume.

**Q : Coût sur EKS ?**
R : Avec Alloy + object storage : souvent moins de 200 $/mois même pour des clusters moyens - voir le cas réel de ce guide pour un exemple précis à ~120 $/mois.

**Q : Comment savoir si ma cardinalité est en train de devenir un problème avant que ça n'explose ?**
R : Surveillez `prometheus_tsdb_symbol_table_size_bytes` et le nombre total de séries actives dans un dashboard dédié - une croissance continue et non expliquée par la croissance réelle de votre infrastructure est le signal d'alerte précoce (section 8).

**Q : Le sampling tail-based vaut-il vraiment la complexité supplémentaire ?**
R : Dès que vous avez déjà eu une fois le problème "la trace de l'incident n'existait pas" (section 8), la réponse est oui sans hésitation - c'est exactement le genre de problème qu'on ne remarque qu'une fois qu'il vous a coûté du temps de debug en pleine crise.

## Conclusion

Tu viens de recevoir la vraie stack d'observabilité que j'installe chez mes clients en 2026 : puissante, économique, et qui permet de dormir tranquille - et cette fois, avec la compréhension complète de pourquoi chaque brique fonctionne comme elle fonctionne, pas juste une liste de commandes à copier.

Ce n'est pas une installation "one-click". C'est une évolution continue. Commence petit (metrics + alerting, avec la cardinalité sous contrôle dès le premier jour), mesure l'impact, puis ajoute logs et traces progressivement, en activant la corrélation entre les trois dès que possible - c'est elle qui transforme trois outils installés côte à côte en une vraie observabilité.

Tu as un cluster qui manque de visibilité ? Des alertes qui fatiguent ton équipe ? Un blocage précis (Alloy config, SLO, cardinalité qui explose) ? Laisse un commentaire détaillé avec ta stack (EKS, bare-metal…), je t'aide personnellement.

Si ce guide t'a aidé à passer à une observabilité pro, partage-le. On monte le niveau ensemble.

On continue à construire des systèmes observables, résilients et professionnels.

## Introduction

**Real Case**: A SaaS client with an EKS infra was spending nights debugging incidents (unexplained 5xx errors). After implementing this stack: mean time to detection dropped from 45 min to under 3 min, and 40% of incidents prevented thanks to predictive alerts. Cost: under $150/month (vs thousands with Datadog).

Open your cluster, grab a coffee, and let's build professional observability together -- all the way, without skimming anything.

## 1. Understanding Observability from A to Z (fundamentals before deploying anything)

Just like in my other guides, let's take the time to understand the mechanics before deploying them. This understanding is what will save you from the two costliest traps in modern observability: uncontrolled cardinality (which can blow up a bill overnight) and alert fatigue (which makes the entire stack useless once nobody trusts the notifications anymore).

### 1.1 The three pillars -- and why you genuinely need all three, not just one

Modern observability rests on three fundamentally different types of signals, and each answers a question the other two can't answer alone:

- **Metrics** (Prometheus): aggregated numeric time series -- answers "**how much**" and "**when**" (how many requests per second, when did latency start climbing). Extremely efficient in storage, but with **zero individual detail** about a specific request.
- **Logs** (Loki): timestamped textual events -- answers "**exactly what**" happened on a given component (the precise error message, the stack trace).
- **Traces** (Tempo): the complete path of **one individual request** across several services -- answers "**where**" time was lost, service by service, in a distributed architecture.

**Why you genuinely need all three**: a latency spike visible in metrics (the "how much") doesn't tell you **which request** or **which service** caused it -- you need a trace for that. And a trace shows you a service took 800ms to respond, but not **why** -- you need that exact service's application log for that. The three pillars aren't redundant, they're **complementary**, and that's exactly why correlation between them (section 1.8) is the real added value of a stack like Grafana, not just having the three tools installed side by side.

### 1.2 Metrics and Prometheus -- the model you really need to understand

Prometheus works on a **pull** model: unlike many systems that passively receive data pushed to them, Prometheus **actively fetches** (scrapes) metrics exposed by each target service, at a regular interval (typically 15-30 seconds), via an HTTP `/metrics` endpoint your application exposes.

**The four metric types, and what genuinely differentiates them**:
- **Counter**: a value that only ever increases (total request count since startup). You never read a counter directly -- you compute its **rate of increase** with `rate()`.
- **Gauge**: a value that can go up or down (number of active connections, memory usage).
- **Histogram**: distributes observations into "buckets" (e.g., how many requests took between 100 and 200ms) -- lets you compute approximate percentiles after the fact.
- **Summary**: similar to histogram, but computes percentiles **client-side** at emission time -- less flexible at query time, but sometimes more precise.

**The two PromQL functions that show up absolutely everywhere, and that you need to master**:

```promql
# rate() : converts a monotonically increasing counter into a per-second rate --
# NEVER read a raw counter value directly, it means nothing on its own
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])

# histogram_quantile() : computes an approximate percentile from histogram buckets --
# this is how you get "p99 latency" from raw bucket data
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
```

**Why `rate()` is essential and not optional**: a raw counter ("there have been 4,582,391 requests since startup") tells you absolutely nothing useful on its own. `rate()` turns that into "how many requests per second on average over the last 5 minutes" -- the only genuinely usable form for understanding recent behavior.

### 1.3 Cardinality -- THE number-one trap almost no tutorial explains

This is the single most important concept in this entire guide, and yet the one least explained elsewhere. A metric's **cardinality** is the number of **unique combinations** of labels it can take. Every unique label combination creates an entirely **distinct time series** stored separately by Prometheus.

Take a concrete and dangerous example:
```
http_requests_total{method="GET", path="/users/12345", status="200"}
http_requests_total{method="GET", path="/users/12346", status="200"}
http_requests_total{method="GET", path="/users/12347", status="200"}
```

If your `path` label contains a **variable user identifier** rather than a generic route pattern (`/users/:id`), you literally create **one time series per user** -- on an application with 100,000 active users, that can represent millions of unique time series, each consuming memory and disk on your Prometheus server. This is exactly the scenario that turns a Prometheus instance from "runs perfectly on 4GB of RAM" into "eats 64GB and falls over" within a few weeks, with no obvious alert flagging it before it's too late.

**The golden rule to absolutely respect**: always normalize your labels toward bounded-cardinality patterns (`/users/:id` rather than the real path with the ID), and **never** put a unique identifier (user ID, request ID, email address) in a metric label -- that information belongs in **logs** or **trace attributes**, never in a metric.

### 1.4 Logs and Loki -- why Loki is radically different from ELK

The fundamental difference between Loki and a system like Elasticsearch: **Loki never indexes your log content**, only its **labels** (exactly like Prometheus indexes metric labels, not the values themselves). The textual content of the log is stored compressed but unindexed.

**What that actually changes**: a Loki search first filters by labels (fast, since indexed -- e.g. `{app="todo-api", environment="prod"}`), **then** scans the text content only within that already-reduced subset. That's infinitely cheaper in storage than a full inverted index on every word of every log line (which is what Elasticsearch does) -- at the cost of somewhat slower text search on very large volumes, a trade-off that's almost always a win for typical infrastructure/application logs.

**A trap to absolutely avoid, symmetric to the one for metrics**: never use a high-cardinality label on your Loki logs either (a `request_id` as a label, say) -- that recreates exactly the same explosion problem as section 1.3, but on the logs side. A `request_id` should be in the log's **content** (searchable as text), never as a label.

### 1.5 Distributed traces -- spans, context, and the delicate art of sampling

A **trace** represents a request's complete journey through your system, made up of several **spans** (each span represents one precise operation -- an HTTP call, a database query -- with a start/end timestamp). Spans are linked together by a **trace context** (a unique trace identifier, propagated from service to service via HTTP headers), which lets you reconstruct the full call tree even across dozens of microservices.

**Sampling -- an unavoidable economic trade-off**: tracing **every single** request individually, at scale, would generate an unmanageable, expensive volume of data. Hence sampling:
- **Head-based sampling**: the decision to trace or not is made **right at the start** of the request (often a simple random percentage, say 1-10%). Simple, but risks missing exactly the interesting requests (the ones that fail or are slow) if the random draw doesn't land on them.
- **Tail-based sampling**: the decision is made **after the fact**, once the request completes, based on its outcome -- you can thereby keep 100% of error or abnormally slow traces, and sample much more aggressively the "normal," uninteresting ones. More powerful, but requires temporarily buffering all spans before deciding (generally done at the OpenTelemetry Collector level).

### 1.6 OpenTelemetry -- the standard, not a tool

A common vocabulary mistake: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is **not a product you install**, it's a **specification and a set of standardized SDKs** for instrumenting code in a vendor-neutral way. You instrument your application **once** with the OpenTelemetry SDK, and can then export that data to Prometheus, Datadog, Tempo, or any OTLP-compatible backend (the standard protocol) -- never needing to re-instrument your code if you switch backends later. That's exactly the opposite of the old "one Prometheus client here, one Datadog client there" approach that locked your code to a specific vendor.

**Auto-instrumentation vs manual instrumentation**: OpenTelemetry SDKs for most languages (Node.js, Python, Java) offer **auto-instrumentation** that automatically patches common libraries (Express, HTTP clients, database drivers) without changing a single line of your business code -- an excellent starting point. Manual instrumentation (creating your own spans around your specific business logic) comes next, only where auto-instrumentation isn't enough.

### 1.7 Grafana Alloy -- why it's genuinely a paradigm shift, not just one more agent

Before Alloy, a typical observability stack required **several separate agents** running side by side on every node: Promtail for logs, Grafana Agent (or node-exporter + a scraper) for metrics, and potentially a separate OpenTelemetry Collector for traces -- each with its own configuration, its own resource footprint, its own maintenance surface.

**Alloy unifies all of that into a single binary, with a single configuration language (River)**, capable of receiving/scraping metrics, logs, AND OTLP traces, transforming them (relabeling, filtering, enrichment), and routing them to Prometheus/Mimir, Loki, and Tempo respectively -- from a single declarative pipeline. Concretely, that means: a single DaemonSet to deploy on your cluster (rather than three), a single configuration to maintain and version, and a single troubleshooting surface the day the collection itself has a problem.

### 1.8 Correlation -- the real added value of this whole stack

The feature that separates a "just installed" observability stack from one genuinely used day to day is **exemplars**: direct links, embedded in a Prometheus metric, pointing to a specific trace that contributed to that measurement. Concretely, looking at a latency spike on a histogram in Grafana, you can click directly on a data point and land on the exact trace of the individual request that caused that spike -- then, from that trace, click on the service involved and land directly on its application logs at the same timestamp. It's this **metric -> trace -> log** triangle, navigable in a few clicks, that turns an incident from "45 minutes digging through scattered logs" into "under 3 minutes" -- exactly the result from this guide's real case.


---

## 2. Global Strategy: The 3 Pillars + Alloy

**Classic mistake I fix everywhere**: install Prometheus alone, then add Loki/Tempo later in chaos. Result: inconsistent configs, labels that don't match across systems, correlation becomes impossible.

**What I do in 2026**:
- **Metrics**: Prometheus (scraping) + remote write to Mimir for long-term
- **Logs**: Loki (light label-based indexing)
- **Traces**: Tempo (ultra-light storage)
- **Unified Collection**: Grafana Alloy (single agent handling everything via OpenTelemetry, section 1.7)
- **Visualization**: Grafana (unified dashboards + alerting)

Benefit: everything in one Grafana UI. Easy correlation (click a log -> trace -> metric, section 1.8).

I always start with metrics + Alloy, then add logs and traces incrementally -- never all three at once on a first deployment, to keep each step independently verifiable.

## 3. Kubernetes Deployment with Helm (Production Approach)

Use **kube-prometheus-stack** (includes Prometheus Operator, Grafana, Alertmanager) + Grafana charts for Loki/Tempo.

Complete, realistic Helm values example for Prometheus + Grafana:
```yaml
prometheus:
  prometheusSpec:
    # Sends samples to Mimir for long-term storage beyond local retention --
    # see section 6 for when this becomes necessary
    remoteWrite:
      - url: "http://mimir-write.example.com/api/v1/push"
        queueConfig:
          maxSamplesPerSend: 5000
    retention: 15d    # local retention -- Mimir handles anything beyond this
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 2Gi
      limits:
        memory: 4Gi   # a hard limit prevents cardinality explosions (section 1.3)
                       # from silently consuming an entire node's memory
    # Discovers ServiceMonitor resources across ALL namespaces automatically --
    # teams can expose their own scrape targets without touching this chart
    serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false
    podMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false

grafana:
  dashboards:
    enabled: true
    defaultDashboardsEnabled: true   # ships the standard k8s/node dashboards immediately
  alerting:
    enabled: true
  additionalDataSources:
    - name: Loki
      type: loki
      url: http://loki-gateway.monitoring.svc:3100
    - name: Tempo
      type: tempo
      url: http://tempo.monitoring.svc:3200
      jsonData:
        tracesToMetrics:
          datasourceUid: prometheus   # enables clicking a trace span -> jump to its metric
        tracesToLogsV2:
          datasourceUid: loki         # enables clicking a trace span -> jump to matching logs

alertmanager:
  alertmanagerSpec:
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi }
```

**What genuinely deserves an explanation here:**
- **`limits.memory` on Prometheus isn't optional**: without a hard cap, a cardinality explosion (section 1.3) progressively consumes all available RAM on the node hosting Prometheus, potentially taking down other pods on that same node. A `limit` turns that scenario into a contained, visible OOMKill (Prometheus restarts, an alert fires), rather than a silent degradation of the whole node.
- **`tracesToMetrics` and `tracesToLogsV2`** on the Tempo datasource are literally what activates the section 1.8 correlation in the Grafana UI -- without these two lines, the three pillars stay installed side by side but never clickably linked.

Install Loki and Tempo (via Grafana charts):
```bash
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm install loki grafana/loki --values loki-values.yaml
helm install tempo grafana/tempo --values tempo-values.yaml
```

**Realistic Loki configuration**, explicitly respecting the section 1.4 cardinality constraint:
```yaml
# loki-values.yaml
loki:
  commonConfig:
    replication_factor: 1   # single-binary mode; raise for HA multi-node setups
  storage:
    type: s3   # object storage -- see section 6 for why this matters at scale
  limits_config:
    # Hard caps preventing a single misconfigured app from creating
    # unbounded label cardinality that would degrade the whole Loki cluster
    max_label_names_per_series: 15
    reject_old_samples: true
    reject_old_samples_max_age: 168h
```

**Grafana Alloy configuration** (replaces Promtail + Grafana Agent), deployed as a DaemonSet, with a complete metrics + logs + traces pipeline in River syntax:

```river
// alloy-config.river

// --- METRICS: discover and scrape every pod annotated for Prometheus scraping ---
discovery.kubernetes "pods" {
  role = "pod"
}

prometheus.scrape "kubernetes_pods" {
  targets    = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets
  forward_to = [prometheus.remote_write.mimir.receiver]
}

prometheus.remote_write "mimir" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://mimir-write.example.com/api/v1/push"
  }
}

// --- LOGS: tail every container log file on the node ---
loki.source.kubernetes "pods_logs" {
  targets    = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets
  forward_to = [loki.write.local.receiver]
}

loki.write "local" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://loki-gateway.monitoring.svc:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
  }
}

// --- TRACES: receive OTLP traces pushed by instrumented applications ---
otelcol.receiver.otlp "default" {
  grpc { endpoint = "0.0.0.0:4317" }
  output {
    traces = [otelcol.exporter.otlp.tempo.input]
  }
}

otelcol.exporter.otlp "tempo" {
  client {
    endpoint = "tempo.monitoring.svc:4317"
    tls { insecure = true }
  }
}
```

**Why this single file concretely replaces three separate configurations**: each block (`prometheus.scrape`, `loki.source.kubernetes`, `otelcol.receiver.otlp`) is a component of the same Alloy pipeline, sharing the same target discovery (`discovery.kubernetes.pods`), the same startup process, the same monitoring surface -- exactly the benefit described in section 1.7. The day you want to add a transformation (say, filtering out noisy logs before sending to Loki), you add a `loki.process` component inline in the same file, never touching a separate system.


## 4. Instrumentation with OpenTelemetry

**What I no longer do**: manually instrument each service with specific Prometheus clients, which locks the code to one particular backend (section 1.6).

**2026 approach**: the OpenTelemetry SDK in your apps (Node.js, Python, Go, etc.), with auto-instrumentation as the first reflex.

Complete, realistic Node.js example:
```ts
// tracing.ts -- imported FIRST, before any other module, so auto-instrumentation
// can patch libraries (express, pg, http) before your app code requires them
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-grpc';
import { Resource } from '@opentelemetry/resources';
import { SemanticResourceAttributes } from '@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions';

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: new Resource({
    // These attributes become searchable trace/log labels across the whole stack --
    // exactly what lets you filter "show me only todo-api in prod" in Grafana
    [SemanticResourceAttributes.SERVICE_NAME]: 'todo-api',
    [SemanticResourceAttributes.DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT]: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  }),
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({
    url: 'http://alloy.monitoring.svc:4317',   // points to Alloy's OTLP receiver (section 3)
  }),
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations()],  // auto-patches express, pg, http, etc.
});

sdk.start();
```

```ts
// index.ts
import './tracing';   // MUST be the very first import in the entire application
import express from 'express';
const app = express();
// ... the rest of your app, completely unmodified
```

**Manual instrumentation for your specific business logic**, once auto-instrumentation is in place:
```ts
import { trace } from '@opentelemetry/api';
const tracer = trace.getTracer('todo-api');

async function computeRecommendations(userId: string) {
  // Creates a custom span visible in Tempo, nested under the auto-instrumented
  // HTTP request span -- gives visibility INTO your business logic, not just the HTTP layer
  return tracer.startActiveSpan('compute-recommendations', async (span) => {
    span.setAttribute('user.id', userId);   // safe here: it's a SPAN attribute, not a metric label (section 1.3)
    try {
      const result = await heavyComputation(userId);
      return result;
    } finally {
      span.end();
    }
  });
}
```

**Why `span.setAttribute('user.id', ...)` is safe here while a Prometheus `user_id` label would be dangerous (section 1.3)**: trace attributes are stored **per individual trace** in Tempo, not aggregated into distinct time series the way Prometheus would. Unbounded cardinality is precisely what traces are designed for (one trace per request, by definition) -- the opposite of metrics, where every label value creates a continuously-stored series.

Alloy receives everything via OTLP and routes it to Prometheus/Loki/Tempo -- your application code never needs to know these three separate backends even exist.

## 5. Dashboards & SLO in Grafana

I always create three categories of dashboards, following the **RED** method (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, and **USE** (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for infrastructure:

- **Infrastructure Dashboard** (USE method): CPU, Memory, Pods, Nodes -- resource utilization and saturation.
- **Application Dashboard** (RED method): Request rate, Error rate, Duration (latency) -- the service's health as seen from outside.
- **Business Dashboard**: custom metrics (todos created, conversion rate) -- the link between technical observability and business value.

### SLOs, done properly -- not just a simple threshold

Add **SLOs** (Service Level Objectives): for instance, 99.9% of requests must respond in under 300ms over a rolling 30-day window. Grafana automatically calculates the remaining **error budget** and can alert when you're burning through it too fast.

**What separates an amateur SLO alert from a professional one**: a naive rule like "alert if error rate exceeds 5% for 5 minutes" either generates too many false positives (a transient 6-minute spike that resolves itself) or misses a real problem that climbs more slowly. The method Google actually uses internally (documented in its SRE Workbook) is **multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting**:

```yaml
# Fires fast for severe, urgent burn (2% of the monthly budget burned in just 1 hour)
- alert: SLOBurnRateCriticalFast
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[5m]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[5m]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    and
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[1h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[1h]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Burning error budget 14.4x too fast -- will exhaust the monthly budget in ~2 days if sustained"

# Fires slower for a sustained, moderate burn over a longer window --
# catches slow leaks the fast rule would never trigger on
- alert: SLOBurnRateWarningSlow
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..", job="todo-api"}[6h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="todo-api"}[6h]))
    ) > (1 * 0.001)
  for: 15m
  labels:
    severity: warning
```

**Why two different windows rather than one**: the short window (5 minutes/1 hour) detects a severe, urgent incident within minutes -- exactly what let this guide's real case go from 45 minutes to under 3 minutes of detection. The long window (6 hours) catches a slow, gradual degradation the short window would completely miss (a sustained 0.15% error rate over hours never crosses the fast rule's threshold, but still exhausts your entire monthly error budget if nobody notices). Combining both is exactly what avoids both noisy false positives and missed real problems.

## 6. Intelligent Alerting with Alertmanager

**Common mistake**: 50 noisy alerts a day that fatigue the team, until nobody actually looks at them anymore (the "alert fatigue" syndrome, essentially identical to the one already detailed in my GitHub Actions guide regarding pipeline notifications).

**My real config**, with grouping, inhibition, and severity-based routing:

```yaml
# alertmanager-config.yaml
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: ['alertname', 'service']
  group_wait: 30s        # waits briefly to batch related alerts into one notification
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h    # don't re-notify on the same unresolved alert every minute
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: critical
      receiver: pagerduty
      continue: false
    - match:
        severity: warning
      receiver: slack
    - match:
        severity: info
      receiver: email

# Prevents a flood of downstream alerts when the real root cause is already known --
# e.g., don't page about every crashing pod if the whole node is already down
inhibit_rules:
  - source_match:
      alertname: NodeDown
    target_match:
      alertname: PodCrashLooping
    equal: ['node']

receivers:
  - name: pagerduty
    pagerduty_configs:
      - service_key: '<pagerduty-integration-key>'
  - name: slack
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: '<slack-webhook-url>'
        channel: '#alerts-warning'
  - name: email
    email_configs:
      - to: 'team@example.com'
  - name: default
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: '<slack-webhook-url>'
        channel: '#alerts-default'
```

**What `inhibit_rules` actually changes**: without this rule, a Kubernetes node going down can trigger **dozens of simultaneous alerts** (one per crashlooping pod on that node), drowning out the genuinely useful alert ("the node is down") under derived noise. With inhibition, only the root alert (`NodeDown`) actually reaches the team -- derived alerts are automatically suppressed as long as the root cause stays active.

Example of a classic Prometheus rule (beyond the SLO already seen in section 5):
```yaml
- alert: HighErrorRate
  expr: rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Error rate above 5% for {{ $labels.service }}"
    runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/high-error-rate"   # always link a runbook
```

**Why always include a `runbook_url`**: an alert that just says "something's wrong" without saying **what to do** transfers the entire cognitive load of resolution to the on-call person, in the middle of the night, under pressure. A link to a documented runbook (initial diagnostic steps, useful commands, escalation contacts) turns a stressful alert into an actionable checklist -- one of the most underrated cultural elements of a good alerting strategy.

## 7. Scaling & 2026 Best Practices

- For more than 50 pods: move to **Mimir** (long-term, highly-available metrics) and store Loki/Tempo on S3/Object Storage rather than local storage.
- Use Grafana Alloy to reduce collection overhead (section 1.7) -- a single agent rather than several mechanically consumes fewer resources per node.
- **Meta-monitoring**: watch the observability stack itself (Prometheus scraping Prometheus, an alert if Alloy stops pushing data) -- without it, you discover your observability is broken only once a real incident hits and nobody sees anything.
- Retention: 15 days for local metrics (Mimir beyond that), 30 days for logs, 7 days for traces (adjust to your compliance needs -- see the scenarios section for regulatory requirements).

**Terraform/GitOps**: version the entire configuration (Helm values, alert rules, dashboards as JSON) with ArgoCD or Flux for multi-environment reproducibility -- exactly the GitOps principle detailed in my dedicated multi-environment guide.


---

## 8. Configuration Scenarios Based on Circumstances -- real-world field expertise

Just like in my other guides, here are the real scenarios I've run into on client projects, and exactly what to do in each case.

### Scenario: your cardinality explodes and your Prometheus bill/memory triples with no obvious reason

**Immediate diagnosis**: use Prometheus's own internal metrics to find the culprit:
```promql
# Ranks every metric name by how many unique label combinations (series) it has --
# the top of this list is almost always your culprit
topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))
```
Once the metric name is identified, look for which label is causing it (often a variable ID in a label like `path`, `user_id`, or `request_id` -- section 1.3). **The fix**: add a `metric_relabel_configs` rule on the scrape config side to drop or normalize the problematic label before ingestion even happens, rather than trying to clean up afterward (which doesn't reclaim memory already consumed by existing series until they naturally expire).

### Scenario: the whole team ignores PagerDuty alerts ("alert fatigue")

**Never add more manual silences as the solution** -- that only temporarily masks the symptom. The real three-step fix: (1) audit every active alert and ask "did anyone actually act differently the last time this fired?" -- if the answer is no, delete it or reclassify it as `severity: info`. (2) Migrate to multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting (section 5) for the remaining critical alerts, which mechanically reduces false positives compared to a simple threshold. (3) Systematically add a `runbook_url` (section 6) to every remaining alert -- an actionable alert with clear steps generates far less fatigue than one that requires rediscovering everything each time.

### Scenario: you need to migrate away from Datadog/New Relic without breaking everything at once

**Never cut the old system before the new one is validated under real conditions.** Run both stacks in parallel for 2-4 weeks: instrument with OpenTelemetry (sections 1.6, 4), which can export **simultaneously** to your old SaaS and to your new self-hosted stack during the transition (dual OTLP export is a standard Collector/Alloy configuration). Compare key metrics between the two systems (error rate, p99 latency) to validate your new instrumentation captures the same reality, before cutting the SaaS subscription.

### Scenario: a regulatory requirement demands log retention of several years

The 30-day retention recommended in section 7 is meant for everyday operational debugging, not compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, local legal obligations that sometimes require 3 to 7 years).

**The solution: separate operational retention from archive retention.** Keep Loki configured for a short, fast-to-query retention (30 days) for daily debugging, but set up S3 lifecycle rules (already detailed in my FinOps guide) that automatically archive older Loki chunks to S3 Glacier -- cheaper, always recoverable for an audit, but deliberately slower to query since that's no longer its main purpose.

### Scenario: an important trace is "missing" and you don't understand why

Nine times out of ten, it's a **sampling** issue (section 1.5): your head-based configuration simply didn't select that exact request to be traced. **The structural fix**: switch to **tail-based** sampling at the Collector/Alloy level, configured to systematically keep 100% of error or abnormally slow traces (beyond a latency threshold), and only aggressively sample "normal" traces with no diagnostic interest. This is a configuration change, not an application code change -- your OpenTelemetry instrumentation stays identical.

### Scenario: you're onboarding a new service and don't know where to start with its observability

**Minimal checklist I systematically apply to any new service**: (1) OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation enabled from the very first deployment (section 4); (2) at minimum, RED metrics exposed (rate, errors, duration -- section 5); (3) a basic dashboard auto-generated from a shared template rather than hand-built every time; (4) at least one basic SLO alert in place before going to production, even a simple one, to be evolved into multi-burn-rate later. A service that ships to production without at least these four elements will, eventually, systematically recreate this guide's original problem: nobody knows what's happening in it anymore.

### Scenario: sensitive data (PII, secrets) accidentally ends up in your logs

**Never rely solely on developer discipline to avoid this** -- a full `console.log(user)` including a password or a card number will, statistically, eventually happen. Configure a `loki.process` component in Alloy with an automatic **redaction** step using regular expressions (card numbers, emails, JWT token patterns) **before** writing to Loki -- a structural protection rather than a simple code review recommendation, in exactly the same spirit as the Gitleaks secret scanning detailed in my GitHub Actions guide, but applied to the log stream rather than the source code.


---

## 9. Real Case: From Blindness to Pro Observability

Scale-up client (EKS, ~200 pods, Node.js microservices):
- Initial problems: no centralized monitoring, incidents discovered by customers before the team itself, debugging that took hours due to no correlation between systems, a Datadog bill judged too high for the perceived value.

**Actions over 3 weeks, in this guide's order:**
1. Deployed kube-prometheus-stack + Alloy via Helm/ArgoCD (sections 2-3)
2. OpenTelemetry instrumentation on all services, auto-instrumentation first (section 4)
3. Loki + Tempo + unified dashboards with correlation enabled (`tracesToMetrics`/`tracesToLogsV2`, section 3)
4. SLO alerts with multi-burn-rate + PagerDuty/Slack routing with inhibition (sections 5-6)
5. **A cardinality fix discovered only afterward**: the payment service had a `transaction_id` label on a custom metric -- exactly the section 1.3 trap, caught thanks to the `topk` query from section 8 during the first week's review, before it had time to genuinely degrade performance.

**Measured results:**
- Mean time to detection: 45 min -> 2 min 40s
- MTTR reduced by 60%
- 40% of incidents prevented (predictive latency/error alerts, via the multi-burn-rate approach from section 5 that catches gradual degradation before it hits a critical threshold)
- Monitoring cost: ~$120/month (S3 + small instances) vs $2,500 with SaaS

The team now says: "We see everything before it explodes" -- and more importantly, they now have the three pillars actually linked together, not just installed side by side.

## 10. 2026 Best Practices -- the complete roadmap

### Cardinality control (the absolute priority)
- **Never a unique identifier as a metric label** -- user ID, request ID, email: that belongs in logs/traces, never in metrics (section 1.3).
- **`metric_relabel_configs` as a systematic guardrail** at the scrape config level, not only as a reaction to an incident that already happened (section 8).
- **Hard limits (`limits.memory`) on Prometheus/Mimir** to turn a cardinality explosion into a contained, visible incident, never a silent degradation of an entire node (section 3).
- **Regular audit with `topk(count by (__name__)(...))`** -- cardinality needs continuous monitoring, not just when the bill surprises you (section 8).

### Alerting and on-call culture
- **Multi-window multi-burn-rate for every critical alert**, never a simple single-window threshold (section 5).
- **Every alert has a `runbook_url`**, no exceptions -- an alert without actionable instructions generates fatigue faster than it helps (section 6).
- **Systematic inhibition** to prevent a root cause from generating dozens of derived alerts (section 6).
- **Quarterly audit of every active alert**: if nobody acted differently the last time it fired, it deserves to be deleted or reclassified (section 8).

### Instrumentation and correlation
- **OpenTelemetry everywhere, auto-instrumentation as the first reflex**, manual instrumentation only for specific business logic (section 4).
- **Correlation explicitly enabled** (`tracesToMetrics`, `tracesToLogsV2`) from the moment Grafana is deployed -- this is the real value of this entire stack, not a secondary configuration detail (section 1.8/3).
- **Tail-based sampling** to never lose an error trace, even while aggressively sampling everything else (section 8).

### Security and compliance
- **Automatic PII/secrets redaction in the log pipeline**, never just a code review recommendation (section 8).
- **Short operational retention + separate archive** for any long-term compliance requirement (section 8).

### Cost and scaling
- **Alloy rather than several separate agents**, systematically (section 1.7).
- **Object storage (S3) for Loki/Tempo as soon as the cluster grows**, never local storage that doesn't scale (section 7).
- **Mimir only when high availability or long retention becomes a genuine need**, not by default on the very first deployment (section 7).

### What field experience teaches you
- **Cardinality is controlled upstream, never downstream** -- a `topk` audit once a month costs 5 minutes; cleaning up an already-established explosion costs days (section 8).
- **An uncorrelated observability stack is just a pile of tools**, not observability -- the clickable metric/trace/log triangle is what genuinely makes the difference mid-incident (section 1.8).
- **Meta-monitoring is never a luxury** -- discovering your observability stack itself is broken in the middle of a critical incident is one of the worst possible moments to find out (section 7).

## Troubleshooting (the problems I run into most often)

- **"My Prometheus memory explodes with no obvious reason"** -> Almost always uncontrolled cardinality (section 1.3) -- immediately run the `topk` query from section 8 to identify the culprit metric/label.
- **"I see no traces despite OpenTelemetry instrumentation"** -> Check that `tracing.ts` (or the equivalent) is imported **first**, before any other import, otherwise auto-instrumentation patches libraries already loaded and has no effect (section 4).
- **"Clicking on a trace doesn't show me the matching logs"** -> Check the `tracesToLogsV2` configuration on the Tempo datasource in Grafana (section 3) -- without it, correlation simply isn't enabled, even if the three systems work individually.
- **"Alertmanager sends a flood of derived alerts during an incident"** -> Check your `inhibit_rules` (section 6) -- a properly identified root cause should automatically suppress derived noise.
- **"A specific trace seems to be missing"** -> Almost always a head-based sampling issue (sections 1.5/8) -- consider switching to tail-based sampling if this becomes recurring on important error traces.

## Production 2026 Monitoring Stack Checklist

- [ ] Deploy Grafana Alloy as a unified agent (metrics + logs + traces)
- [ ] Install Prometheus Operator + remote write (Mimir if HA/long retention is needed)
- [ ] Hard memory limits configured to contain any cardinality explosion
- [ ] Add Loki for logs with controlled labels and cardinality limits
- [ ] Configure Tempo for OpenTelemetry traces with appropriate sampling (tail-based if possible)
- [ ] OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation on all services
- [ ] Create unified dashboards in Grafana (RED method for services, USE for infra)
- [ ] Enable correlation (`tracesToMetrics`, `tracesToLogsV2`)
- [ ] Define SLOs with multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting
- [ ] Configure Alertmanager with intelligent routing + inhibition + linked runbooks
- [ ] Automatic PII/secrets redaction in the log pipeline
- [ ] Meta-monitor the stack itself
- [ ] Version everything with GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux)
- [ ] Test end-to-end metrics/logs/traces correlation
- [ ] Document incident runbooks

## FAQ

**Q: I'm a beginner, where do I start?**
A: Alloy + Prometheus + Grafana, with a genuine understanding of cardinality (section 1.3) from day one -- it's the trap that costs the most to fix after the fact. Add Loki then Tempo once comfortable. That already covers 80% of needs.

**Q: Prometheus or Mimir?**
A: Prometheus to start. Move to Mimir when you need high availability and long retention (beyond 15-30 days), typically past 50 pods (section 7).

**Q: Loki vs ELK?**
A: Loki is much lighter and cheaper for Kubernetes workloads, thanks to label-only indexing rather than a full inverted index (section 1.4). ELK remains relevant for very structured logs requiring complex text search at very large volume.

**Q: Cost on EKS?**
A: With Alloy + object storage: often under $200/month even for medium clusters -- see this guide's real case for a precise example at ~$120/month.

**Q: How do I know if my cardinality is becoming a problem before it explodes?**
A: Watch `prometheus_tsdb_symbol_table_size_bytes` and the total active series count in a dedicated dashboard -- continuous growth not explained by your infrastructure's actual growth is the early warning sign (section 8).

**Q: Is tail-based sampling really worth the added complexity?**
A: Once you've already had the "the incident's trace didn't exist" problem (section 8) even once, the answer is an unhesitating yes -- it's exactly the kind of problem you only notice once it's already cost you debugging time mid-crisis.

## Conclusion

You just received the real observability stack I install for my clients in 2026: powerful, cost-effective, and that lets you sleep peacefully -- and this time, with the full understanding of why every building block works the way it does, not just a list of commands to copy.

It's not a one-click install. It's continuous evolution. Start small (metrics + alerting, with cardinality under control from day one), measure the impact, then progressively add logs and traces, enabling correlation between the three as early as possible -- that's what turns three tools installed side by side into genuine observability.

Have a cluster lacking visibility? Alerts that fatigue your team? A specific blocker (Alloy config, SLO, exploding cardinality)? Leave a detailed comment with your stack (EKS, bare-metal...), I'll help you personally.

If this guide helped you move to pro observability, share it. Let's raise the bar together.

Let's keep building observable, resilient, and professional systems.

contentFr:
## Résumé Visuel : Les 12 Phases de Hardening que J'Applique en 2026

| Phase | Objectif Principal | Outils Clés | Niveau de Protection |
|-------|--------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| 1     | Premier accès & root | Mot de passe fort, hostname | Ferme la porte la plus évidente |
| 2     | Compte admin & SSH | Clés Ed25519, port custom, no root | Bloque 95 % des scans automatiques |
| 3     | Base système | Updates auto, sysctl, outils essentiels | Réduit les vulnérabilités connues |
| 4     | Firewall simple | UFW default deny | Surface d'attaque minimale, mise en place rapide |
| 5     | Firewall avancé | iptables + persistance | Contrôle fin, anti-spoofing, anti-SYN-flood |
| 6     | Protection réactive | Fail2Ban + recidive | Bannissement automatique local |
| 7     | Reverse proxy | Nginx durci + Let's Encrypt | Base HTTPS saine avant tout filtrage applicatif |
| 8     | Firewall système avancé | CSF + LFD | Rate limiting + détection de scan de ports |
| 9     | Détection collaborative | CrowdSec + bouncers | Intelligence partagée entre millions de serveurs |
| 10    | WAF applicatif | Naxsi (whitelist) | Protection contre injections SQL, XSS |
| 11    | Protection CDN | Cloudflare + bouncer | DDoS & bots bloqués avant le serveur |
| 12    | Hardening final | Headers, Monit, Lynis, rapports | Forteresse maintenable dans la durée |

**Pourquoi cette approche est celle que j'utilise vraiment en 2026 ?**
Je ne fais plus confiance à une seule couche. J'empile SSH durci → UFW → iptables → Fail2Ban → Nginx → CSF → CrowdSec → Naxsi → Cloudflare. Résultat : un serveur qui résiste aux scans massifs, aux bots et aux attaques ciblées, tout en restant facile à maintenir au quotidien.

> 💡 Si tu veux comprendre le **pourquoi** derrière chaque couche - l'analogie du château fort, réactif vs proactif, whitelist vs blacklist - j'ai écrit un article dédié à ça. Ici, l'objectif est différent : avoir **sous les yeux**, phase par phase, la procédure exacte à exécuter du premier accès jusqu'à la forteresse complète, sans détour, comme un vrai runbook qu'on suit une commande après l'autre.
