## 2. Stratégie Globale : Separation CI vs CD + GitOps

**Erreur courante** : tout faire dans GitHub Actions (build + deploy direct). Résultat : pipeline fragile et pas auditable, exactement le problème détaillé en section 1.1.

**Ce que je fais en 2026** :
- **CI** (GitHub Actions) : build image Docker, tests unitaires/E2E, security scan (Trivy), push vers registry (GHCR ou ECR).
- **CD** (ArgoCD) : GitOps - ArgoCD surveille le repo Git et applique les manifests.
- **Progressive Delivery** : Argo Rollouts gère Blue-Green (switch instantané) ou Canary (traffic progressif + analysis).

Flux : PR → Preview env → Merge develop → Staging (Canary) → Merge main → Prod (Blue-Green ou Canary contrôlé).

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (CI)

Voici mon workflow réel, complet :

```yaml
name: CI - Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [develop, main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [develop, main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Tests run INSIDE the exact image that will ship -- never against
      # a separate "test build" that could subtly differ from production
      - name: Run tests inside the built image
        run: docker run --rm myapp:${{ github.sha }} npm test

      - name: Trivy security scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          format: 'table'
          exit-code: '1'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'

      - name: Login to GHCR
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        run: |
          docker tag myapp:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # This is where CI ends and GitOps takes over -- no kubectl, no helm,
      # just a commit to a separate repo (section 1.1)
      - name: Update GitOps repo
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        run: |
          git clone https://x-access-token:${{ secrets.GITOPS_TOKEN }}@github.com/my-org/gitops-repo.git
          cd gitops-repo
          ENV=$([ "${{ github.ref }}" = "refs/heads/main" ] && echo "prod" || echo "staging")
          yq -i ".spec.template.spec.containers[0].image = \"ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}\"" environments/$ENV/rollout.yaml
          git commit -am "Deploy ${{ github.sha }} to $ENV"
          git push
```

**Ce que ce workflow fait de bien, et pourquoi c'est important** : les tests s'exécutent **à l'intérieur** de l'image Docker déjà buildée, jamais sur un environnement de test séparé - vous testez exactement le binaire qui va partir en production, pas un artefact potentiellement différent. Le job **s'arrête** après avoir mis à jour le dépôt GitOps - jamais de `kubectl apply` ni d'accès direct au cluster depuis GitHub Actions, exactement le principe de séparation CI/CD de la section 1.1.

## 4. ArgoCD + Argo Rollouts pour Zero Downtime

Je déploie ArgoCD en GitOps, puis j'utilise **Argo Rollouts** au lieu de `Deployment` classique - un `Deployment` standard ne supporte ni Blue-Green ni Canary avec analysis, seulement un rolling update basique.

### Blue-Green, avec pre/post-promotion analysis (mon choix principal en Prod pour les services critiques)

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    blueGreen:
      activeService: myapp-active
      previewService: myapp-preview      # lets you test the new version internally BEFORE the real switch
      autoPromotionEnabled: false        # requires explicit approval, or a passing analysis, before switching
      scaleDownDelaySeconds: 30          # keeps the old ReplicaSet warm briefly, for instant rollback (section 1.2)
      prePromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: smoke-test     # runs against previewService before any real traffic is switched
      postPromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: success-rate   # keeps watching AFTER the switch, can auto-rollback if it degrades
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: ghcr.io/my-org/myapp:latest
          readinessProbe:                 # mandatory -- see section 1.4
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:                      # mandatory for graceful shutdown -- see section 1.5
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }
```

### Canary avec analysis Prometheus (mon choix par défaut en Staging, et en Prod pour les services non critiques)

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: "2m" }
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: "5m" }
        - setWeight: 100
```

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result < 0.05
      failureLimit: 3     # after 3 consecutive failed checks, automatically abort and roll back
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="myapp", version="canary", status=~"5.."}[1m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="myapp", version="canary"}[1m]))
```

**Ce qui distingue ce manifeste d'une config de départ trop simpliste** : `prePromotionAnalysis` valide la nouvelle version **avant** qu'elle ne reçoive du vrai trafic (un smoke test contre le `previewService`), tandis que `postPromotionAnalysis` continue de surveiller **après** la bascule et peut déclencher un rollback automatique si un problème apparaît seulement sous charge réelle - un smoke test seul ne détecterait jamais un problème qui n'apparaît qu'après plusieurs minutes de trafic réel.

ArgoCD synchronise automatiquement dès qu'il détecte le changement d'image dans le dépôt GitOps (le commit poussé à la fin du workflow CI de la section 3) - exactement le mécanisme `selfHeal`/réconciliation continue déjà détaillé dans mon guide multi-environnements.


## 5. Feature Flags & Preview Environments

Je découple toujours "deploy" et "release" avec Unleash ou LaunchDarkly - exactement le mécanisme détaillé en profondeur dans mon guide multi-environnements : le code peut être en production sans être actif pour tout le monde.

**Pourquoi les feature flags et le Canary sont complémentaires, pas redondants** : le Canary limite l'exposition **au niveau infrastructure** (quel pourcentage de requêtes touche le nouveau code, indépendamment de qui elles concernent), les feature flags limitent l'exposition **au niveau fonctionnel** (quel utilisateur précis voit quelle fonctionnalité, indépendamment du pourcentage de trafic servi par la nouvelle version). Combiner les deux vous donne un contrôle à deux dimensions : vous pouvez avoir 100% du trafic sur la nouvelle version de code (Canary terminé) tout en n'activant une fonctionnalité risquée que pour 1% des utilisateurs (flag), ou l'inverse.

**Preview environment pour chaque PR**, via un ArgoCD `ApplicationSet` qui génère dynamiquement une Application par PR ouverte :

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: myapp-previews
spec:
  generators:
    # Automatically watches open PRs on the repo and generates one Application per PR
    - pullRequest:
        github:
          owner: my-org
          repo: myapp
        requeueAfterSeconds: 60
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'myapp-preview-{{number}}'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/gitops-repo.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: environments/preview
        helm:
          parameters:
            - name: image.tag
              value: 'pr-{{head_sha}}'
      destination:
        namespace: 'preview-pr-{{number}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
        syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]
```

**Ce que ce générateur `pullRequest` fait concrètement** : ArgoCD interroge périodiquement l'API GitHub, détecte automatiquement chaque PR ouverte, et crée (ou met à jour, ou détruit à la fermeture de la PR) une Application ArgoCD complète et isolée pour chacune - namespace éphémère dédié, aucune intervention manuelle nécessaire. C'est l'automatisation complète de ce qui était fait à la main (ou via un script GitHub Actions séparé) dans une approche moins mature.

## 6. Rollback & Observabilité

- **Rollback manuel** : `kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp` (annule immédiatement un rollout en cours, revient à la version stable précédente) ou un simple `git revert` sur le dépôt GitOps (ArgoCD resynchronise automatiquement vers l'état antérieur).
- **Rollback automatique** : géré par `analysis` (sections 4) - si `failureLimit` est dépassé, Argo Rollouts annule automatiquement le rollout sans aucune intervention humaine, souvent avant même qu'un humain n'ait eu le temps de remarquer une alerte.
- **Observabilité** : intégration Prometheus pour l'analysis (error rate, latence) - voir mon guide monitoring dédié pour le détail complet de la stack d'observabilité qui alimente ces requêtes (cardinalité, corrélation, SLO).

**Le vrai avantage du rollback Blue-Green par rapport au Canary** : avec Blue-Green et `scaleDownDelaySeconds` configuré (section 4), l'ancien ReplicaSet reste **chaud et prêt** pendant une fenêtre après la bascule - un rollback consiste juste à re-router le `activeService` vers lui, sans jamais avoir besoin de reconstruire ou redémarrer quoi que ce soit. C'est ce qui explique le "rollback en moins de 10 secondes" du cas réel de ce guide.

## 7. Cas de configuration selon les circonstances - la vraie compétence de terrain

Comme dans mes autres guides, voici les scénarios réels rencontrés sur des projets clients, et exactement quoi faire dans chaque cas.

### Scénario : votre déploiement nécessite une migration de base de données

**Ne déployez jamais le changement de schéma et le changement de code applicatif dans le même rollout.** Suivez toujours le pattern Expand-Contract de la section 1.7 en trois déploiements Argo Rollouts séparés et espacés dans le temps : (1) migration additive seule (nouvelle colonne, nullable ou avec valeur par défaut) ; (2) code applicatif qui écrit dans les deux structures, lit depuis la nouvelle avec repli sur l'ancienne ; (3) une fois 100% du trafic stabilisé sur le nouveau code depuis plusieurs jours, suppression de l'ancienne structure. Chaque étape est elle-même déployée avec le Canary/Blue-Green habituel - la prudence structurelle de l'Expand-Contract et la prudence du rollout progressif se combinent, elles ne se remplacent pas l'une l'autre.

### Scénario : votre service est stateful et le Blue-Green semble trop coûteux ou risqué

Un service avec état local significatif (des WebSockets avec état en mémoire, un cache local non partagé) ne se prête pas bien à un doublement brutal de capacité ni à un switch instantané qui abandonnerait des connexions actives.

**La solution : un Canary avec un drainage de connexions particulièrement soigné plutôt qu'un Blue-Green.** Configurez une `pause` plus longue à chaque palier (section 4) pour laisser le temps aux connexions longues de se terminer naturellement sur l'ancienne version pendant que le trafic **nouveau** bascule progressivement vers la nouvelle, plutôt que de forcer une coupure nette. Pour des WebSockets en particulier, envisagez un message applicatif de "reconnexion gracieuse" envoyé aux clients avant la fermeture (section 1.5), plutôt que de compter uniquement sur le mécanisme SIGTERM/preStop générique.

### Scénario : une analysis Canary reste bloquée sans jamais conclure

**Symptôme classique** : le rollout reste indéfiniment sur un palier intermédiaire (10%, 50%), sans jamais avancer ni échouer explicitement. **Cause quasi systématique** : la requête Prometheus de l'`AnalysisTemplate` ne retourne tout simplement aucune donnée - un label mal orthographié, un nom de métrique qui a changé, ou (plus insidieux) un trafic si faible sur le palier en cours que la requête sur une fenêtre courte n'a littéralement aucune donnée sur laquelle statuer. **La solution** : testez systématiquement chaque requête PromQL d'`AnalysisTemplate` manuellement dans Grafana **avant** de la déployer dans un manifeste de production, et prévoyez un seuil de trafic minimum en dessous duquel le palier avance automatiquement sans attendre une analysis statistiquement non significative.

### Scénario : vous devez déployer pendant un pic de trafic (impossible de reporter)

**Réduisez la taille du premier palier Canary plutôt que de l'annuler** : sur un pic de trafic, même 5% de trafic représente un volume absolu de requêtes bien plus élevé qu'en temps normal - largement suffisant pour une analysis statistiquement significative en quelques minutes plutôt que les 10-15 minutes habituelles nécessaires en trafic faible. Profitez-en pour raccourcir les `pause` entre paliers (le signal arrive plus vite avec plus de volume), tout en gardant `postPromotionAnalysis` actif plus longtemps qu'en temps normal, puisque c'est justement le moment où un problème de charge a le plus de chances de se révéler.

### Scénario : vous devez faire un rollback Blue-Green après que l'ancien ReplicaSet a déjà été scale-down

Si `scaleDownDelaySeconds` (section 4) s'est déjà écoulé, l'ancien ReplicaSet n'existe plus - un rollback "instantané" n'est alors plus possible, il faut redéployer l'ancienne version depuis zéro (avec un nouveau cold start de tous les pods).

**La leçon structurelle** : dimensionnez `scaleDownDelaySeconds` en fonction de votre **vraie confiance** dans le nouveau déploiement, pas d'une valeur par défaut arbitraire - pour un changement particulièrement risqué (une migration de base de données en cours, un changement d'architecture majeur), augmentez généreusement ce délai (plusieurs heures, voire un jour complet) plutôt que de vous fier au réglage par défaut de quelques secondes qui convient très bien pour un changement de routine mais pas pour un changement à risque élevé.

### Scénario : vous voulez tester votre pipeline de rollback avant d'en avoir vraiment besoin

**Ne testez jamais un mécanisme de rollback pour la première fois en pleine crise réelle.** Intégrez un exercice de **chaos engineering ciblé** (déjà mentionné dans mon guide multi-environnements) directement sur le pipeline de déploiement lui-même : en Staging, déployez délibérément une version qui échoue son `AnalysisTemplate` (un taux d'erreur artificiellement injecté), et vérifiez que le rollback automatique se déclenche bien, dans le délai attendu, sans intervention manuelle. Faites cet exercice à intervalle régulier (trimestriel, par exemple), pas une seule fois à la mise en place initiale - une configuration d'alerte ou d'analysis peut se dégrader silencieusement avec le temps (un dashboard renommé, une métrique dépréciée) sans que personne ne le remarque avant le jour où on en a réellement besoin.

## 8. Cas Réel : Passage à du Vrai Zero Downtime

Client scale-up (EKS, microservices Node.js) :
- Avant : déploiements manuels, downtime 3-8 min à chaque déploiement, rollback long et stressant (souvent plus de 20 minutes, nécessitant de reconstruire une image depuis un ancien commit).

**Actions mises en place, dans l'ordre de ce guide :**
1. Séparation CI (GitHub Actions) / CD (ArgoCD GitOps) - section 1.1/3
2. Migration de `Deployment` classique vers `Rollout` Argo, avec probes de readiness et `preStop` hook correctement configurés pour la première fois (sections 1.4-1.5) - **un correctif qui a, à lui seul, éliminé une bonne partie du downtime observé auparavant**, indépendamment même de la stratégie Blue-Green/Canary.
3. Blue-Green en Prod pour les services critiques (switch < 10s), avec `scaleDownDelaySeconds` dimensionné à 5 minutes (section 7)
4. Canary en Staging avec analysis Prometheus pour tout changement de routine (section 4)
5. Feature flags Unleash pour découpler le rythme de déploiement du rythme de mise en visibilité auprès des utilisateurs (section 5)
6. Adoption du pattern Expand-Contract (section 1.7) pour toute migration de schéma - a éliminé une classe entière d'incidents de compatibilité qui touchait auparavant environ un déploiement sur cinq

**Résultats mesurés :**
- 10+ déploiements/jour (contre 1 par semaine avant)
- MTTR réduit de 70 %
- Zéro downtime utilisateur mesuré sur 6 mois consécutifs
- Rollback moyen : moins de 10 secondes en Blue-Green (contre plus de 20 minutes avant)

L'équipe dit maintenant : "On push en prod comme on push en dev" - et surtout, elle a arrêté de redouter les déploiements du vendredi, qui sont devenus des déploiements comme les autres.

## 9. Bonnes pratiques 2026 - la feuille de route complète

### Mécanique de zero downtime (les fondations non négociables)
- **Readiness ET liveness probes correctement configurées sur chaque service**, jamais optionnelles - c'est le mécanisme qui empêche structurellement le routage vers un pod pas encore prêt (section 1.4).
- **Gestion explicite de SIGTERM avec drainage de connexions**, dans le code applicatif lui-même - sans ça, aucune stratégie de rollout, aussi sophistiquée soit-elle, n'évite les coupures de requêtes en vol (section 1.5).
- **`preStop` hook systématique** pour absorber le délai de propagation réseau entre le retrait des endpoints et l'arrêt réel du pod (section 1.5).
- **PodDisruptionBudget sur chaque service critique**, pour protéger la disponibilité pendant les perturbations volontaires de l'infrastructure, pas seulement pendant vos propres déploiements (section 1.6).

### Migrations de données
- **Expand-Contract systématique pour tout changement de schéma**, jamais un changement destructif en une seule étape (section 1.7).
- **Compatibilité descendante du code applicatif** pendant toute la fenêtre de coexistence ancien/nouveau - le nouveau code doit savoir lire l'ancien format aussi longtemps que l'ancien code peut encore tourner.

### Stratégie de rollout
- **Blue-Green pour les changements à haut risque et les services critiques**, Canary par défaut pour le reste - exactement le même arbitrage que celui détaillé dans mon guide multi-environnements.
- **`prePromotionAnalysis` ET `postPromotionAnalysis`**, jamais l'un sans l'autre - un problème peut n'apparaître que sous charge réelle, bien après la bascule (section 4).
- **`scaleDownDelaySeconds` dimensionné selon le risque réel du changement**, jamais une valeur par défaut universelle (section 7).
- **Testez chaque requête PromQL d'AnalysisTemplate manuellement avant production**, et prévoyez un seuil de trafic minimum pour éviter les analyses statistiquement non significatives (section 7).

### Culture et validation continue
- **Testez le mécanisme de rollback lui-même régulièrement**, en conditions contrôlées, jamais seulement en pleine crise réelle pour la première fois (section 7).
- **Feature flags pour découpler déploiement et visibilité utilisateur**, systématiquement pour tout changement fonctionnel à risque (section 5).
- **Preview environments automatisés pour chaque PR**, jamais un environnement de test partagé et goulot d'étranglement (section 5).

### Ce que l'expérience terrain apprend
- **Les probes mal configurées causent plus de "faux downtime" que les stratégies de rollout elles-mêmes** - avant même de choisir Blue-Green ou Canary, vérifiez que vos probes reflètent vraiment l'état de préparation de votre application (section 8).
- **Une migration de base de données mal préparée est la cause numéro un des vrais incidents de production**, bien plus que les stratégies de déploiement elles-mêmes - investissez-y le temps que ça mérite, jamais en dernière minute (section 1.7).
- **Le vrai gain business du zero downtime n'est pas la disponibilité en elle-même, c'est la vélocité qu'elle libère** - une équipe qui ne redoute plus ses déploiements en fait naturellement beaucoup plus souvent, et corrige donc les problèmes plus tôt, en plus petits incréments (section 8).

## Dépannage (les problèmes que je rencontre le plus souvent)

- **"Des requêtes échouent pendant le déploiement malgré Argo Rollouts bien configuré"** → Vérifiez en premier le graceful shutdown côté application (section 1.5) - c'est de loin la cause la plus fréquente de downtime "malgré" une stratégie de rollout correcte.
- **"Le rollout reste bloqué sur un palier Canary indéfiniment"** → Testez la requête PromQL de l'`AnalysisTemplate` manuellement dans Grafana (section 7) - neuf fois sur dix, elle ne retourne simplement aucune donnée.
- **"Le rollback ne semble pas instantané malgré le Blue-Green"** → Vérifiez que `scaleDownDelaySeconds` n'est pas déjà écoulé (section 7) - l'ancien ReplicaSet doit encore exister pour permettre un rollback réellement instantané.
- **"Un déploiement casse la prod après une migration de schéma"** → Vérifiez que le pattern Expand-Contract a bien été respecté (section 1.7) - un changement destructif en une seule étape est presque toujours la cause.
- **"Le preview environment d'une PR ne se crée jamais"** → Vérifiez les permissions du token GitHub utilisé par le générateur `pullRequest` de l'ApplicationSet (section 5), et que le webhook/polling ArgoCD fonctionne bien vers votre organisation GitHub.

## Checklist CI/CD Zero Downtime 2026

- [ ] Séparation stricte CI (GitHub Actions) / CD (ArgoCD GitOps)
- [ ] Readiness ET liveness probes configurées sur chaque service
- [ ] Gestion explicite de SIGTERM avec drainage de connexions dans le code
- [ ] `preStop` hook configuré sur chaque Rollout
- [ ] PodDisruptionBudget sur chaque service critique
- [ ] Pattern Expand-Contract pour toute migration de schéma
- [ ] Argo Rollouts (Blue-Green ou Canary) plutôt que Deployment classique
- [ ] `prePromotionAnalysis` ET `postPromotionAnalysis` configurées
- [ ] Requêtes PromQL d'AnalysisTemplate testées manuellement avant production
- [ ] `scaleDownDelaySeconds` dimensionné selon le risque réel du changement
- [ ] Feature flags pour découpler déploiement et release
- [ ] Preview environments automatisés via ApplicationSet
- [ ] Rollback testé régulièrement en conditions contrôlées
- [ ] Monitoring du pipeline lui-même (meta-monitoring)

## FAQ

**Q : Par où commencer si mon pipeline actuel fait encore du downtime ?**
R : Ne commencez jamais par la stratégie de rollout (Blue-Green/Canary) - commencez par les fondations de la section 1 : readiness probes correctement configurées, puis gestion de SIGTERM (section 1.4-1.5). C'est souvent là que se cache la majorité du downtime actuel, avant même de toucher à Argo Rollouts.

**Q : Blue-Green ou Canary, comment choisir concrètement pour mon service ?**
R : Blue-Green pour les changements à haut risque avec besoin d'un rollback réellement instantané (une migration de base de données en cours, un changement d'architecture majeur) ; Canary par défaut pour le reste, moins coûteux en ressources et détecte les problèmes progressivement plutôt que sur 100% du trafic d'un coup - voir mon guide multi-environnements pour le tableau de décision complet.

**Q : Comment gérer une migration de base de données sans casser le zero downtime ?**
R : Le pattern Expand-Contract en trois déploiements séparés (section 1.7) - jamais un changement de schéma destructif dans le même déploiement que le changement de code applicatif.

**Q : Mon rollback n'est pas vraiment instantané malgré Blue-Green, pourquoi ?**
R : Vérifiez `scaleDownDelaySeconds` (section 7) - si l'ancien ReplicaSet a déjà été supprimé, un "rollback instantané" nécessite en réalité de redéployer depuis zéro.

**Q : Faut-il un service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) pour faire du Canary correctement ?**
R : Non, obligatoire seulement si vous avez besoin d'un split de trafic précis au pourcentage exact (section 1.3) - sans service mesh, Argo Rollouts approxime le pourcentage via le ratio de pods, largement suffisant pour la majorité des cas d'usage.

## Conclusion

Tu viens de recevoir le vrai pipeline CI/CD zero-downtime que j'utilise sur mes projets clients en 2026 : sécurisé, rapide, observable et maintenable - et surtout, avec la compréhension complète du mécanisme technique qui rend le "zero downtime" possible, pas juste une liste d'outils à assembler.

Ce n'est pas parfait du premier jour. Commence par les fondations (probes, graceful shutdown - section 1), puis le CI + ArgoCD simple, puis ajoute Rollouts et analysis progressivement. Teste en Staging avant Prod, et teste ton mécanisme de rollback lui-même avant d'en avoir vraiment besoin.

Tu as un pipeline qui fait encore du downtime ? Un blocage avec Argo Rollouts ou analysis ? Une migration de base de données qui t'inquiète ? Laisse un commentaire détaillé avec ta stack (EKS, bare-metal, etc.), je regarde ça avec toi personnellement.

Si ce guide t'a aidé à passer à des déploiements sereins et fréquents, partage-le. On monte le niveau de delivery ensemble.

On continue à construire des systèmes rapides, résilients et professionnels.

Grab your coffee, open your repo, and let's build a pro pipeline together.

## 1. What "Zero Downtime" Actually Means (fundamentals before the pipeline)

Just like in my other guides, let's take the time to understand the mechanics before assembling them. "Zero downtime" isn't a magic property of a tool -- it's the result of several precise mechanisms that must **all** be correct at the same time. Getting even one of them wrong recreates downtime, even with Argo Rollouts perfectly configured otherwise.

### 1.1 CI vs CD -- a distinction too often blurred

**CI (Continuous Integration)** answers "is this code valid?" (build, tests, security scan). **CD (Continuous Deployment/Delivery)** answers a completely different question: "how do we get this validated code all the way to production, safely?". Mixing both into a single pipeline (GitHub Actions doing both the build AND a direct `kubectl apply` to prod) recreates exactly the push-based problem detailed in my multi-environment guide: your CI then needs direct, broad access to your production cluster -- a considerable attack surface for what should remain a simple artifact builder.

**The clean separation**: GitHub Actions stops after pushing a validated Docker image and updating a tag in a GitOps repository. ArgoCD, running inside the cluster, takes over from there -- exactly the pull-based model already covered in depth in my multi-environment guide.

### 1.2 Blue-Green -- the real mechanism behind the "instant switch"

Technically, a Blue-Green deployment never switches "infrastructure" -- it switches a **Kubernetes Service selector**. Two complete ReplicaSets run simultaneously (the old "Blue" and the new "Green"), each with its own set of pods, and a single Kubernetes Service object routes actual traffic to one or the other based on its `selector`. Argo Rollouts automates this switch: it creates the new ReplicaSet, waits for it to be **healthy** (section 1.4), first exposes it via a `previewService` (for internal testing before the real switch), then, on approval (manual or via `analysis`), reconfigures the `activeService` to point to the new ReplicaSet -- a few-millisecond change at the Kubernetes control-plane level, which explains the "instant switch."

**The real hidden cost of Blue-Green**: during the transition window, you're paying for **twice the compute capacity** (the old AND new ReplicaSets run in parallel) -- exactly the trade-off already covered in my multi-environment guide, but one you absolutely need to budget for before choosing this strategy for a resource-heavy service.

### 1.3 Canary -- how traffic is actually split

Contrary to a common assumption, Kubernetes itself has **no native concept of traffic percentage**. A classic Kubernetes Service just routes uniformly to every pod matching its selector. Argo Rollouts simulates a traffic percentage in a more subtle way: it adjusts the **relative number of pods** in the old and new ReplicaSets to approximate the desired percentage (10% traffic ≈ 10% of active pods out of the total), unless a **service mesh** (Istio, Linkerd) or a **canary-aware Ingress Controller** (NGINX with canary annotations) is configured to do a true request-by-request traffic split, far more precise than the pod-ratio approximation.

**What you really need to remember**: without a service mesh or a canary-aware Ingress, your "10% traffic" is actually a statistical rounding based on pod count, not a true deterministic guarantee -- good enough for most use cases, but worth knowing before relying on an exact percentage for a critical decision.

### 1.4 Readiness and Liveness Probes -- why they're non-negotiable, not just "recommended"

This is the point the original version of this guide mentioned in one line ("readiness/liveness probes mandatory") without ever explaining why -- and it's precisely the mechanism that **structurally prevents** Kubernetes from routing traffic to a pod that isn't ready yet.

- **Readiness probe**: answers "is this pod ready to receive traffic **right now**?". A pod that fails its readiness probe is **immediately removed** from the Service's endpoints -- no request is routed to it, without ever being restarted because of it.
- **Liveness probe**: answers "is this pod in a healthy state, or does it need to be restarted?". A pod that fails its liveness probe is **killed and recreated** by Kubernetes.

**The direct link to zero downtime**: without a properly configured readiness probe, Argo Rollouts (or even a classic Deployment) considers a new pod "ready" as soon as its container starts -- potentially before your application has finished connecting to its database or warming its cache. Result: real requests fail against a pod that's technically "up" but not actually functional yet. That's exactly the kind of silent downtime people wrongly blame on "a deployment bug" when it's really a misconfigured probe.

### 1.5 Graceful Shutdown and connection draining -- the most commonly forgotten mechanism

Here's THE concept most cruelly missing from the original version of this guide, and yet it accounts for a good chunk of "mysterious" downtime in practice.

When Kubernetes removes a pod (a scale-down after a Blue-Green switch, for instance), here's the actual sequence:
1. The pod is removed from the Service's endpoints (no more **new** requests are routed to it).
2. Kubernetes sends a **SIGTERM** signal to the container's main process.
3. A **grace period** starts (30 seconds by default) -- the pod keeps running, letting requests **already in flight** complete normally.
4. If the process hasn't stopped on its own by the end of the grace period, Kubernetes sends a brutal **SIGKILL**.

**The classic trap**: if your application never explicitly handles SIGTERM (it just ignores the signal, or dies instantly without finishing in-flight requests), you cut active connections mid-response -- exactly the kind of "intermittent downtime hard to reproduce" that makes an incident particularly frustrating to diagnose.

```ts
// graceful-shutdown.ts -- the missing piece almost every zero-downtime guide skips
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  console.log('SIGTERM received, draining connections...');
  server.close(() => {
    // Only exit once every in-flight HTTP request has actually completed
    console.log('All connections drained, exiting');
    process.exit(0);
  });
});
```

**And the `preStop` hook, even more subtle**: between the moment the pod is removed from endpoints (step 1) and the moment SIGTERM is actually sent, there's a short network propagation delay (kube-proxy, the Ingress Controller, a service mesh all need to be notified). Without care, requests can still arrive at that pod **right after** its removal from endpoints but **before** SIGTERM is received. The standard fix: a `preStop` hook that waits a few seconds before SIGTERM is actually sent, giving network propagation time to finish everywhere:

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]   # gives kube-proxy/ingress time to stop
                                          # routing new traffic before SIGTERM hits
```

### 1.6 PodDisruptionBudget -- protecting availability during voluntary disruptions

A **PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)** guarantees a minimum number (or percentage) of an application's pods stays available during **voluntary** infrastructure disruptions (a node upgrade, a manual scale-down) -- but **not** during involuntary failures (a node crash), which nothing can structurally prevent.

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: myapp-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 80%   # never let voluntary disruptions drop below 80% of replicas at once
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
```

**The link to zero downtime**: without a PDB, a cluster maintenance operation (an EKS node upgrade, say) could legitimately evict several of your application's pods **simultaneously**, potentially all of them if the timing is unlucky. The PDB forces Kubernetes to respect your minimum threshold, spreading evictions out over time rather than all at once.

### 1.7 Database migrations -- the real challenge of zero downtime

This is the most technically delicate point in this entire guide, and yet completely absent from the original version. The problem: during a progressive rollout (Canary) or even a Blue-Green switch, **both the old AND the new version of your code run simultaneously** for a window of time -- meaning **both** need to work correctly against the **same database schema** at the same time.

**The standard solution: the Expand-Contract pattern**, across three separate deployments rather than one:
1. **Expand**: add the new column/table without ever touching the old one -- both the old AND the new code still work, since nothing existing has changed.
2. **Migrate**: deploy the new code that uses the new structure, while **temporarily writing to both** (the old AND the new column) to maintain backward compatibility while traffic is being cut over.
3. **Contract**: once the cutover is complete and validated for a while, remove the old column/table in a separate, later deployment.

**Why it takes three deployments and not one**: a deployment that renames a column in a single step instantly breaks the old version of the code still active during the progressive rollout (it looks for a column that no longer exists) -- exactly the class of bug that never shows up in testing (where only one version of the code is active at a time) but systematically breaks in a real Canary/Blue-Green rollout.


---

## 2. Global Strategy: CI vs CD Separation + GitOps

**Common mistake**: doing everything in GitHub Actions (build + direct deploy). Result: a fragile, unauditable pipeline, exactly the problem detailed in section 1.1.

**What I do in 2026**:
- **CI** (GitHub Actions): build the Docker image, unit/E2E tests, security scan (Trivy), push to registry (GHCR or ECR).
- **CD** (ArgoCD): GitOps -- ArgoCD watches the Git repo and applies the manifests.
- **Progressive Delivery**: Argo Rollouts handles Blue-Green (instant switch) or Canary (progressive traffic + analysis).

Flow: PR -> Preview env -> Merge develop -> Staging (Canary) -> Merge main -> Prod (Blue-Green or controlled Canary).

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (CI)

My real, complete workflow:

```yaml
name: CI - Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [develop, main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [develop, main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Tests run INSIDE the exact image that will ship -- never against
      # a separate "test build" that could subtly differ from production
      - name: Run tests inside the built image
        run: docker run --rm myapp:${{ github.sha }} npm test

      - name: Trivy security scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          format: 'table'
          exit-code: '1'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'

      - name: Login to GHCR
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        run: |
          docker tag myapp:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # This is where CI ends and GitOps takes over -- no kubectl, no helm,
      # just a commit to a separate repo (section 1.1)
      - name: Update GitOps repo
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.ref == 'refs/heads/develop'
        run: |
          git clone https://x-access-token:${{ secrets.GITOPS_TOKEN }}@github.com/my-org/gitops-repo.git
          cd gitops-repo
          ENV=$([ "${{ github.ref }}" = "refs/heads/main" ] && echo "prod" || echo "staging")
          yq -i ".spec.template.spec.containers[0].image = \"ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}\"" environments/$ENV/rollout.yaml
          git commit -am "Deploy ${{ github.sha }} to $ENV"
          git push
```

**What this workflow gets right, and why it matters**: tests run **inside** the already-built Docker image, never on a separate test environment -- you're testing the exact binary that ships to production, not a potentially different artifact. The job **stops** after updating the GitOps repo -- never a `kubectl apply` or direct cluster access from GitHub Actions, exactly the CI/CD separation principle from section 1.1.

## 4. ArgoCD + Argo Rollouts for Zero Downtime

Deploy ArgoCD in GitOps mode, then use **Argo Rollouts** instead of a classic `Deployment` -- a standard `Deployment` supports neither Blue-Green nor Canary with analysis, only a basic rolling update.

### Blue-Green, with pre/post-promotion analysis (my main choice in Prod for critical services)

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    blueGreen:
      activeService: myapp-active
      previewService: myapp-preview      # lets you test the new version internally BEFORE the real switch
      autoPromotionEnabled: false        # requires explicit approval, or a passing analysis, before switching
      scaleDownDelaySeconds: 30          # keeps the old ReplicaSet warm briefly, for instant rollback (section 1.2)
      prePromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: smoke-test     # runs against previewService before any real traffic is switched
      postPromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: success-rate   # keeps watching AFTER the switch, can auto-rollback if it degrades
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: ghcr.io/my-org/myapp:latest
          readinessProbe:                 # mandatory -- see section 1.4
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:                      # mandatory for graceful shutdown -- see section 1.5
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }
```

### Canary with Prometheus analysis (my default choice in Staging, and in Prod for non-critical services)

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: "2m" }
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: "5m" }
        - setWeight: 100
```

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result < 0.05
      failureLimit: 3     # after 3 consecutive failed checks, automatically abort and roll back
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="myapp", version="canary", status=~"5.."}[1m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="myapp", version="canary"}[1m]))
```

**What sets this manifest apart from an overly simplistic starting config**: `prePromotionAnalysis` validates the new version **before** it ever gets real traffic (a smoke test against the `previewService`), while `postPromotionAnalysis` keeps watching **after** the switch and can trigger an automatic rollback if a problem only shows up under real load -- a smoke test alone would never catch a problem that only appears after several minutes of real traffic.

ArgoCD automatically syncs the moment it detects the image change in the GitOps repo (the commit pushed at the end of the section 3 CI workflow) -- exactly the `selfHeal`/continuous reconciliation mechanism already covered in depth in my multi-environment guide.


## 5. Feature Flags & Preview Environments

I always decouple "deploy" from "release" with Unleash or LaunchDarkly -- exactly the mechanism detailed in depth in my multi-environment guide: code can be in production without being active for everyone.

**Why feature flags and Canary are complementary, not redundant**: Canary limits exposure **at the infrastructure level** (what percentage of requests hits the new code, regardless of who they belong to), feature flags limit exposure **at the functional level** (which specific user sees which feature, regardless of what percentage of traffic the new code version is serving). Combining both gives you two-dimensional control: you can have 100% of traffic on the new code version (Canary complete) while only enabling a risky feature for 1% of users (flag), or the reverse.

**Preview environment for every PR**, via an ArgoCD `ApplicationSet` that dynamically generates one Application per open PR:

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: myapp-previews
spec:
  generators:
    # Automatically watches open PRs on the repo and generates one Application per PR
    - pullRequest:
        github:
          owner: my-org
          repo: myapp
        requeueAfterSeconds: 60
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'myapp-preview-{{number}}'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/gitops-repo.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: environments/preview
        helm:
          parameters:
            - name: image.tag
              value: 'pr-{{head_sha}}'
      destination:
        namespace: 'preview-pr-{{number}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
        syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]
```

**What this `pullRequest` generator actually does**: ArgoCD periodically queries the GitHub API, automatically detects every open PR, and creates (or updates, or destroys upon PR closure) a complete, isolated ArgoCD Application for each one -- a dedicated ephemeral namespace, no manual intervention needed. It's the complete automation of what used to be done by hand (or via a separate GitHub Actions script) in a less mature setup.

## 6. Rollback & Observability

- **Manual rollback**: `kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp` (immediately cancels an in-progress rollout, reverting to the previous stable version) or a simple `git revert` on the GitOps repo (ArgoCD automatically resyncs to the prior state).
- **Automatic rollback**: handled by `analysis` (section 4) -- if `failureLimit` is exceeded, Argo Rollouts automatically aborts the rollout with zero human intervention, often before a human even has time to notice an alert.
- **Observability**: Prometheus integration for analysis (error rate, latency) -- see my dedicated monitoring guide for the full detail of the observability stack feeding these queries (cardinality, correlation, SLOs).

**The real advantage of Blue-Green rollback over Canary**: with Blue-Green and `scaleDownDelaySeconds` configured (section 4), the old ReplicaSet stays **warm and ready** for a window after the switch -- a rollback is just re-routing the `activeService` back to it, never needing to rebuild or restart anything. That's what explains this guide's real case's "rollback in under 10 seconds."


---

## 7. Configuration Scenarios Based on Circumstances -- real-world field expertise

Just like in my other guides, here are the real scenarios I've run into on client projects, and exactly what to do in each case.

### Scenario: your deployment requires a database migration

**Never deploy a schema change and an application code change in the same rollout.** Always follow the Expand-Contract pattern from section 1.7 across three separate, time-spaced Argo Rollouts deployments: (1) an additive-only migration (a new column, nullable or with a default value); (2) application code that writes to both structures, reading from the new one with a fallback to the old; (3) once 100% of traffic has been stable on the new code for several days, removal of the old structure in a separate deployment. Each step is itself deployed with the usual Canary/Blue-Green process -- the structural caution of Expand-Contract and the caution of a progressive rollout combine, they don't replace one another.

### Scenario: your service is stateful and Blue-Green feels too costly or risky

A service with significant local state (WebSockets with in-memory state, a local, unshared cache) doesn't lend itself well to a sudden capacity doubling or an instant switch that would drop active connections.

**The solution: a Canary with particularly careful connection draining rather than Blue-Green.** Configure a longer `pause` at each step (section 4) to give long-lived connections time to naturally end on the old version while **new** traffic progressively shifts to the new one, rather than forcing a clean cutoff. For WebSockets specifically, consider an application-level "graceful reconnect" message sent to clients before closing (section 1.5), rather than relying solely on the generic SIGTERM/preStop mechanism.

### Scenario: a Canary analysis stays stuck without ever concluding

**Classic symptom**: the rollout stays indefinitely on an intermediate step (10%, 50%), never advancing nor explicitly failing. **Almost systematic cause**: the `AnalysisTemplate`'s Prometheus query simply returns no data at all -- a mistyped label, a metric name that changed, or (more insidiously) traffic so low on the current step that the query over a short window literally has nothing to compute on. **The fix**: always manually test every `AnalysisTemplate` PromQL query in Grafana **before** deploying it in a production manifest, and set a minimum traffic threshold below which the step advances automatically rather than waiting on a statistically meaningless analysis.

### Scenario: you need to deploy during a traffic peak (can't postpone)

**Shrink the first Canary step rather than canceling it entirely**: during a traffic peak, even 5% traffic represents a far higher absolute request volume than usual -- more than enough for a statistically significant analysis in a few minutes rather than the usual 10-15 minutes needed under light traffic. Take the opportunity to shorten the `pause` between steps (the signal arrives faster with more volume), while keeping `postPromotionAnalysis` active longer than usual, since that's exactly when a load-related problem is most likely to surface.

### Scenario: you need to roll back a Blue-Green deployment after the old ReplicaSet has already been scaled down

If `scaleDownDelaySeconds` (section 4) has already elapsed, the old ReplicaSet no longer exists -- an "instant" rollback is no longer possible; you have to redeploy the old version from scratch (with a fresh cold start of every pod).

**The structural lesson**: size `scaleDownDelaySeconds` based on your **actual confidence** in the new deployment, not an arbitrary default value -- for a particularly risky change (an in-progress database migration, a major architectural change), generously increase this delay (several hours, even a full day) rather than relying on a default of a few seconds that's fine for a routine change but not for a high-risk one.

### Scenario: you want to test your rollback pipeline before you genuinely need it

**Never test a rollback mechanism for the first time in the middle of a real crisis.** Integrate a targeted **chaos engineering** exercise (already mentioned in my multi-environment guide) directly on the deployment pipeline itself: in Staging, deliberately deploy a version that fails its `AnalysisTemplate` (an artificially injected error rate), and verify the automatic rollback actually triggers, within the expected timeframe, with no manual intervention. Run this exercise on a regular schedule (quarterly, say), not just once during initial setup -- an alerting or analysis configuration can silently degrade over time (a renamed dashboard, a deprecated metric) without anyone noticing until the day you genuinely need it.


---

## 8. Real Case: Achieving Genuine Zero Downtime

Scale-up client (EKS, Node.js microservices):
- Before: manual deployments, 3-8 min downtime on every deployment, a slow and stressful rollback process (often over 20 minutes, requiring rebuilding an image from an old commit).

**Actions implemented, in this guide's order:**
1. Separated CI (GitHub Actions) from CD (ArgoCD GitOps) -- section 1.1/3
2. Migrated from a classic `Deployment` to an Argo `Rollout`, with readiness probes and a `preStop` hook properly configured for the first time (sections 1.4-1.5) -- **a fix that, on its own, eliminated a good chunk of the previously observed downtime**, even before the Blue-Green/Canary strategy itself came into play.
3. Blue-Green in Prod for critical services (switch < 10s), with `scaleDownDelaySeconds` sized to 5 minutes (section 7)
4. Canary in Staging with Prometheus analysis for every routine change (section 4)
5. Unleash feature flags to decouple deployment cadence from user-facing release cadence (section 5)
6. Adopted the Expand-Contract pattern (section 1.7) for every schema migration -- eliminated an entire class of compatibility incidents that previously affected roughly one deployment out of five

**Measured results:**
- 10+ deployments/day (vs 1 per week before)
- MTTR reduced by 70%
- Zero user-facing downtime measured over 6 consecutive months
- Average rollback: under 10 seconds on Blue-Green (vs over 20 minutes before)

The team now says: "We push to prod like we push to dev" -- and more importantly, they stopped dreading Friday deployments, which became deployments like any other.

## 9. 2026 Best Practices -- the complete roadmap

### Zero-downtime mechanics (the non-negotiable foundations)
- **Readiness AND liveness probes properly configured on every service**, never optional -- it's the mechanism that structurally prevents routing to a pod that isn't ready yet (section 1.4).
- **Explicit SIGTERM handling with connection draining**, in the application code itself -- without it, no rollout strategy, however sophisticated, avoids dropped in-flight requests (section 1.5).
- **Systematic `preStop` hook** to absorb the network propagation delay between endpoint removal and the pod's actual shutdown (section 1.5).
- **PodDisruptionBudget on every critical service**, to protect availability during voluntary infrastructure disruptions, not just during your own deployments (section 1.6).

### Data migrations
- **Systematic Expand-Contract for every schema change**, never a destructive change in a single step (section 1.7).
- **Backward compatibility of application code** throughout the old/new coexistence window -- the new code must be able to read the old format for as long as the old code might still be running.

### Rollout strategy
- **Blue-Green for high-risk changes and critical services**, Canary by default for everything else -- exactly the same trade-off detailed in my multi-environment guide.
- **Both `prePromotionAnalysis` AND `postPromotionAnalysis`**, never just one -- a problem might only show up under real load, well after the switch (section 4).
- **`scaleDownDelaySeconds` sized to the change's actual risk**, never a universal default (section 7).
- **Test every `AnalysisTemplate` PromQL query manually before production**, and set a minimum traffic threshold to avoid statistically meaningless analyses (section 7).

### Culture and continuous validation
- **Test the rollback mechanism itself regularly**, under controlled conditions, never only for the first time during a real crisis (section 7).
- **Feature flags to decouple deployment from user visibility**, systematically for any risky functional change (section 5).
- **Automated preview environments for every PR**, never a shared test environment that becomes a bottleneck (section 5).

### What field experience teaches you
- **Misconfigured probes cause more "fake downtime" than the rollout strategies themselves** -- before even choosing Blue-Green or Canary, verify your probes genuinely reflect your application's actual readiness (section 8).
- **A poorly prepared database migration is the number-one cause of real production incidents**, far more than the deployment strategies themselves -- invest the time it deserves, never as a last-minute afterthought (section 1.7).
- **The real business win of zero downtime isn't availability itself, it's the velocity it unlocks** -- a team that no longer dreads its deployments naturally does them much more often, and therefore fixes problems earlier, in smaller increments (section 8).

## Troubleshooting (the problems I run into most often)

- **"Requests fail during deployment despite Argo Rollouts being well-configured"** -> Check application-side graceful shutdown first (section 1.5) -- by far the most common cause of downtime "despite" a correct rollout strategy.
- **"The rollout stays stuck on a Canary step indefinitely"** -> Manually test the `AnalysisTemplate`'s PromQL query in Grafana (section 7) -- nine times out of ten it simply returns no data.
- **"Rollback doesn't seem instant despite Blue-Green"** -> Check whether `scaleDownDelaySeconds` has already elapsed (section 7) -- the old ReplicaSet needs to still exist for a genuinely instant rollback.
- **"A deployment breaks prod after a schema migration"** -> Check whether the Expand-Contract pattern was actually followed (section 1.7) -- a destructive single-step change is almost always the cause.
- **"A PR's preview environment never gets created"** -> Check the GitHub token permissions used by the ApplicationSet's `pullRequest` generator (section 5), and that ArgoCD's webhook/polling is properly working against your GitHub organization.

## Ultimate Zero Downtime CI/CD Checklist 2026

- [ ] Strict CI (GitHub Actions) / CD (ArgoCD GitOps) separation
- [ ] Readiness AND liveness probes configured on every service
- [ ] Explicit SIGTERM handling with connection draining in the code
- [ ] `preStop` hook configured on every Rollout
- [ ] PodDisruptionBudget on every critical service
- [ ] Expand-Contract pattern for every schema migration
- [ ] Argo Rollouts (Blue-Green or Canary) rather than a classic Deployment
- [ ] Both `prePromotionAnalysis` AND `postPromotionAnalysis` configured
- [ ] AnalysisTemplate PromQL queries manually tested before production
- [ ] `scaleDownDelaySeconds` sized to the change's actual risk
- [ ] Feature flags to decouple deployment and release
- [ ] Automated preview environments via ApplicationSet
- [ ] Rollback tested regularly under controlled conditions
- [ ] Monitoring of the pipeline itself (meta-monitoring)

## FAQ

**Q: Where do I start if my current pipeline still has downtime?**
A: Never start with the rollout strategy (Blue-Green/Canary) -- start with the section 1 foundations: properly configured readiness probes, then SIGTERM handling (sections 1.4-1.5). That's often where most of the current downtime hides, well before you even touch Argo Rollouts.

**Q: Blue-Green or Canary, how do I actually choose for my service?**
A: Blue-Green for high-risk changes needing a genuinely instant rollback (an in-progress database migration, a major architectural change); Canary by default for everything else, cheaper in resources and detects problems progressively rather than on 100% of traffic at once -- see my multi-environment guide for the full decision table.

**Q: How do I handle a database migration without breaking zero downtime?**
A: The Expand-Contract pattern across three separate deployments (section 1.7) -- never a destructive schema change in the same deployment as the application code change.

**Q: My rollback isn't truly instant despite Blue-Green, why?**
A: Check `scaleDownDelaySeconds` (section 7) -- if the old ReplicaSet has already been deleted, a "instant rollback" actually requires redeploying from scratch.

**Q: Do I need a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) to do Canary correctly?**
A: No, only mandatory if you need a precise, exact-percentage traffic split (section 1.3) -- without a service mesh, Argo Rollouts approximates the percentage via pod ratio, which is more than enough for most use cases.

## Conclusion

You just received the real zero-downtime CI/CD pipeline I use on client projects in 2026: secure, fast, observable, and maintainable -- and more importantly, with the full understanding of the technical mechanism that makes "zero downtime" possible, not just a list of tools to assemble.

It's not perfect from day one. Start with the foundations (probes, graceful shutdown -- section 1), then simple CI + ArgoCD, then progressively add Rollouts and analysis. Always test in Staging before Prod, and test your rollback mechanism itself before you genuinely need it.

Have a pipeline that still causes downtime? Stuck on Argo Rollouts or analysis? A database migration that worries you? Leave a detailed comment with your stack (EKS, bare-metal, etc.), I'll look at it with you personally.

If this guide helped you achieve calm, frequent deployments, share it. Let's raise delivery standards together.

Let's keep building fast, resilient, and professional systems.
